paper_pattern: AIBE is a 100-question MCQ test; the 10-part plan divides it into ten blocks of 10 questions each. Part 4 = 8 questions from IPC/BNS + 2 from Company Law.
Pass mark is a percentage of total marks (currently understood as 45 percent for General/OBC and 40 percent for SC/ST/PwD) [VERIFY against the latest BCI notification].
No negative marking has been the practice, so never leave a question blank.
examiner_objectives: Test whether a fresh advocate can identify the correct offence on given facts (practice-readiness), not whether they can recite whole sections.
Test knowledge of the new criminal codes: since 1 July 2024 trials for new offences run under BNS, so the exam now mixes IPC and BNS references.

Test fundamentals that never change: mens rea, general exceptions, murder versus culpable homicide, common intention versus common object, abetment, attempt, theft-extortion-robbery-dacoity ladder, cheating versus criminal breach of trust.
Test landmark cases that shaped criminal law (Bachan Singh, Virsa Singh, Nanavati, Barendra Kumar Ghosh, Gian Kaur, Kedar Nath, Tukaram, Jacob Mathew).
Test awareness of current legal developments (new BNS offences, sedition replacement, mob lynching, organised crime, community service, marital rape debate).

bns_at_a_glance.summary: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 replaced the Indian Penal Code, 1860 for offences committed on or after 1 July 2024. IPC continues to govern offences committed before that date (Article 20(1) and BNS s.531-type savings).
headline_facts_per_government_statement: 358 sections (IPC had 511) arranged in 20 chapters (IPC had 23).

About 20 new offences added; imprisonment increased for about 33 offences; fine increased for about 83; mandatory minimum punishment in about 23 offences; community service for 6 offences; about 19 provisions repealed.
Women and children offences are brought up front in Chapter V (ss.63-99); offences affecting the human body follow in Chapter VI (ss.100-146).
Sedition (IPC 124A) is not retained as such; BNS 152 punishes acts endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity of India.
Adultery (IPC 497) and unnatural offences between adults (IPC 377) are omitted, reflecting Joseph Shine (2018) and Navtej Johar (2018).
Attempt to commit suicide (IPC 309) is dropped; a narrow offence survives in BNS 226 (attempt to commit suicide to compel or restrain a public servant).

ipc_bns_sections.title: Fundamentals: Territorial Jurisdiction, Mens Rea, Stages of Crime, Definitions
key_points: Territorial operation: BNS s.1(4)-(5) (IPC ss.2-4): every person is liable for acts or omissions in India; extra-territorial reach covers Indian citizens abroad, offences on ships or aircraft registered in India, and offences targeting a computer resource located in India.
Check the exact wording of BNS s.1(4)-(5) in the bare act for the extra-territorial provisions [VERIFY].
Crime = Actus reus + Mens rea + Injury (harm) + Human being. Maxim: actus non facit reum nisi mens sit rea. Statutory offences may impose strict liability (State of Maharashtra v MH George, 1965).

Four stages: Intention, Preparation, Attempt, Accomplishment. Preparation is generally not punishable, except for specific offences (waging war, dacoity preparation, counterfeiting, possession of counterfeit instruments).

Definitions (BNS s.2): 'child' means under 18 years; 'gender' includes male, female and transgender; 'dishonestly' = intention of causing wrongful gain or wrongful loss; 'fraudulently' = intent to defraud; 'reason to believe'; 'voluntarily'; 'document' now expressly includes electronic and digital records; 'movable property'; 'valuable security'; 'counterfeit'.
Wrongful gain/loss means gain/loss by unlawful means of property to which the gainer is not legally entitled (retaining or keeping out).
Act (s.2) includes illegal omission; 'Illegal' covers everything that is an offence or prohibited by law or gives ground for civil action.

General explanations (BNS s.3): s.3(5) common intention (IPC 34); s.3(6) criminal act by several persons; s.3(7) co-operation by doing one of several acts; s.3(8) effect caused partly by act and partly by omission; s.3(9) act done by several persons.

Sentences and Chapter II: s.4 lists punishments: death, life imprisonment, imprisonment (rigorous or simple), forfeiture of property, fine and community service (new). s.5 commutation (death to life or not less than 7 years; life to not less than 7 years). s.6 life imprisonment treated as 20 years for fractions of terms. Solitary confinement limits in ss.11-12 (not exceeding 14 days at a time, not more than 3 months overall in the scale).

Community service is a punishment in only six provisions: ss.202 (public servant unlawfully engaging in trade), 209 (non-attendance in obedience to summons), 226 (attempt to commit suicide to compel or restrain public servant), 303(2) (petty theft, first offender, value under Rs 5,000, property returned), 355 (drunken misconduct in public), 356(2) (defamation).

case_laws.case: State of Maharashtra v M.H. George (1965)
case_laws.principle: Mens rea is not required where a statute (FERA/RBI notification) imposes strict liability; but mens rea is presumed unless excluded by clear words.

case_laws.case: Nathulal v State of MP (1966)
case_laws.principle: Mens rea is the essence of a crime; for storing foodgrains without licence, honest belief in compliance mattered.

case_laws.case: Aher Raja Khima v State of Saurashtra (1955)
case_laws.principle: Even where mens rea is a requirement, 'knowledge' includes the capacity to foresee consequences.

case_laws.case: Abhayanand Mishra v State of Bihar (1961)
case_laws.principle: Preparation ends and attempt begins when the accused commits the first overt act towards the offence (false representation in an application).

exam_traps: Preparation is not punishable unless the Code says so; the first positive step towards the offence is attempt.
A child is anyone under 18 under BNS, but the doli incapax age for criminal responsibility is still 7 (and 7-12 with immaturity).
'Community service' appears only six times: do not select it as a punishment for ordinary theft or hurt.

mcqs.q: Under BNS, community service as punishment is provided for which offence?
mcqs.explain: BNS 356(2) lists community service for defamation; IPC 500 lacked it.

mcqs.q: For purposes of calculating fractions of terms of punishment, life imprisonment is reckoned as:
mcqs.explain: BNS s.6 (IPC s.57) treats life imprisonment as equivalent to 20 years.

mcqs.q: Which stage of crime is, as a rule, not punishable?
mcqs.explain: Intention alone and, usually, preparation are not punishable; attempt and accomplishment are.

ipc_bns_sections.title: General Exceptions (Chapter III, BNS ss.14-44)
key_points: Structure: judicial and legal acts (14-16), mistake of fact (14, 17), accident (18), necessity (19), infancy (20-21), insanity (22), intoxication (23-24), consent (25-31), compulsion (32), trifling harm (33), private defence (34-44).
Mistake of fact (s.14, 17) protects a person who by reason of mistake of FACT (not law) believes himself bound by law or justified. Ignorantia juris non excusat.
Judicial acts: judge acting judicially in exercise of power he in good faith believes he has (s.15); acts done pursuant to a judgment or order of court (s.16).

Accident (s.18): act done by accident or misfortune, without criminal intention or knowledge, in doing a lawful act in a lawful manner by lawful means with proper care. Tunda v Rex (1950): death in a sudden fight with lawful blow is not accident if intention is present.

Necessity (s.19): act likely to cause harm but done without criminal intent to prevent other harm to person or property is no offence, if the harm prevented is greater and there is good faith. Example: ship captain steers to save more lives. Dudley & Stephens (1884): necessity is no defence to murder.

Infancy: below 7 years: absolute immunity (s.20); 7-12 years: immunity if the child has not attained sufficient maturity to understand the nature and consequence of conduct (s.21). Above 12 years: full liability under BNS, but juvenile justice law (JJ Act 2015) governs persons below 18.

Insanity (s.22): at the time of doing the act, by reason of unsoundness of mind, the person is incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that it is wrong or contrary to law. The M'Naghten rules. Legal insanity, not medical insanity. Burden of proof is on the accused (Evidence Act/BSA), but only on preponderance of probability (Dahyabhai Chhaganbhai Thakkar, 1964). Irresistible impulse is not recognised.

Intoxication: involuntary intoxication (administered without knowledge or against will) is a defence if it makes the person incapable of knowing the nature of the act (s.23). Voluntary intoxication is not a defence, but intention or knowledge is assessed as if sober for knowledge; for specific intent, the court may consider whether intoxication prevented the formation of intent (Basdev v State of PEPSU, 1956).

Consent: s.25 (consent to suffer harm short of death, e.g., boxing, surgery), s.26 (act in good faith for benefit of a person with consent, even if risk of death: surgery), s.27 (child under 12 or person of unsound mind: guardian's consent), s.28 (consent under fear of injury or misconception of fact is no consent), s.29 (acts offences independent of harm: abortion cannot be justified by consent), s.30 (act in good faith for benefit without consent when it is impossible to get consent), s.31 (communication in good faith, e.g., doctor informing patient).

Consent limits: no consent can justify causing death (except private defence, and surgery done in good faith with consent under s.26). Consent given by a person below 12 or of unsound mind is invalid. Consent for sexual acts: BNS rape provisions fix 18 years as age of consent.

Compulsion (s.32): threat of instant death compels act, except murder and offences against the State punishable by death. Duress must be present, not future. Example: a person forced at gunpoint to join a robbery cannot claim s.32 if he voluntarily placed himself in the situation.
Trifling harm (s.33): harm so slight that no person of ordinary sense and temper would complain (de minimis).

Private defence (ss.34-44): right to defend one's own body and property and those of others against offences (s.34-35). No right against lawful acts of public servants acting in good faith under colour of office (s.37), except where there is reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt.

Private defence of body extends to causing death only against: (1) assault causing reasonable apprehension of death, (2) grievous hurt, (3) rape, (4) [IPC 100 also listed an assault with intent to gratify unnatural lust; BNS omits it because IPC 377 was dropped] [VERIFY], (5) kidnapping or abduction, (6) wrongful confinement with apprehension of inability to seek public aid, (7) acid attack (s.38).

Private defence of property extends to causing death against robbery, house-breaking by night, arson (mischief by fire to human dwelling), theft/mischief/house-trespass causing apprehension of death or grievous hurt (s.41).

Right commences when reasonable apprehension of danger arises and continues as long as apprehension continues. Right does not include inflicting more harm than necessary (s.34/35; excess leads to murder Exception 2 if death results).
No right of private defence when there is time to have recourse to public authorities (s.37(4)).

Section 44 (IPC 106): when the right of private defence of life is exercised against a deadly assault, the defender may run the risk of harm to an innocent person if he cannot otherwise exercise the right.

case_laws.case: Darshan Singh v State of Punjab (2010)
case_laws.principle: Supreme Court laid down ten guidelines on private defence: it is preventive not punitive, the accused need not prove it beyond reasonable doubt (preponderance suffices), danger must be real and imminent, and weapon injuries are assessed on the apprehension, not on precise measurement.

case_laws.case: Vidhya Singh v State of MP (1971)
case_laws.principle: Burden on accused to prove private defence is lighter; the right cannot be weighed in golden scales.

case_laws.case: Jai Dev v State of Punjab (1963)
case_laws.principle: Right of private defence cannot be exercised once the threat has ceased; right is available only to repel aggression.

case_laws.case: Mohinder Pal Jolly v State of Punjab (1979)
case_laws.principle: Firing at a mob, when the danger to property alone existed and no death apprehension, exceeds private defence.

case_laws.case: Dahyabhai Chhaganbhai Thakkar v State of Gujarat (1964)
case_laws.principle: Burden of proving insanity is on accused, but only to the standard of preponderance of probabilities; unsoundness must exist at the time of act.

case_laws.case: Hari Singh Gond v State of MP (2008)
case_laws.principle: Legal insanity vs. medical insanity: only cognitive incapacity at the time of the act matters.

case_laws.case: Basdev v State of PEPSU (1956)
case_laws.principle: Voluntary drunkenness is not a defence; intention must be assessed taking account of the effect of drink on the capacity to form it.

case_laws.case: Dudley & Stephens (1884)
case_laws.principle: Necessity is no defence to murder.

case_laws.case: Tunda v Rex (1950)
case_laws.principle: A blow in a sudden quarrel is not 'accident' where intent to cause injury is present.

case_laws.case: Reg v Govinda (1876)
case_laws.principle: Mistake of fact vs. intention in culpable homicide (classic exposition of s.299 vs 300).

exam_traps: Mistake of fact is a defence; mistake of law is not.
Insanity: the test is incapacity to know nature of act or that it is wrong/contrary to law; irresistible impulse and moral insanity are not enough.

The right of private defence never extends to causing more harm than necessary, and for property alone it extends to death only in the listed offences (robbery, house-breaking by night, arson, theft/mischief/trespass causing death/grievous hurt apprehension).
No private defence against lawful acts of public servants even if the act may not be strictly justifiable, if done in good faith under colour of office.
Compulsion under s.32 is not a defence to murder or offences against the State punishable by death.

mcqs.q: A child aged 9 who has not attained sufficient maturity commits an act. Under BNS, which provision protects him?
mcqs.explain: s.21 (IPC 83) covers a child between 7 and 12 years of insufficient maturity.

mcqs.q: The right of private defence of body extends to causing death in case of:
options: Assault causing apprehension of grievous hurt
mcqs.explain: BNS 38 lists apprehension of death or grievous hurt among the cases where death may be caused.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a defence to a charge of murder?
mcqs.explain: Dudley & Stephens: necessity is not a defence to murder.

mcqs.q: Burden of proving the plea of insanity lies on:
mcqs.explain: The accused must prove it by preponderance of probabilities.

ipc_bns_sections.title: Joint and Constructive Liability: Common Intention (s.3(5)) and Unlawful Assembly / Common Object (s.190)
key_points: Section 3(5) BNS (IPC 34) lays down a rule of evidence and joint liability: when a criminal act is done by several persons in furtherance of the common intention of all, each is liable as if he alone did it.

Ingredients: (1) criminal act by several persons; (2) common intention of all; (3) participation by each in the act. Common intention requires a PRE-ARRANGED PLAN and prior meeting of minds, but it may be formed on the spot (Pandurang v State of Hyderabad, 1955).
Section 3(5) creates no substantive offence; it only attributes liability. Section 149 (BNS 190) also creates constructive liability but is more extensive in scope.
Mahbub Shah v Emperor (1945, Privy Council): common intention implies a pre-arranged plan; mere presence is insufficient.

Barendra Kumar Ghosh v Emperor (1925): the Privy Council held that a person who merely stood guard ('they also serve who only stand and wait') shares the common intention and is liable for the act of the principal offender.

Common object (s.190, IPC 149): if an offence is committed by any member of an unlawful assembly in prosecution of the common object, every member is liable if the offence was likely to be committed in prosecution of the common object (BNS wording tracks IPC).

Unlawful assembly (s.189): five or more persons with a common object of any listed kind: overawing the government/public servant by criminal force, resisting execution of law, committing mischief or criminal trespass, obtaining possession of property by criminal force, or compelling a person to do what he is not legally bound to do.
Rioting (s.191): force or violence used by an unlawful assembly or a member of it in prosecution of the common object. Rioting armed with a deadly weapon is a graver offence.

Distinctions: s.3(5) needs common INTENTION; s.190 needs common OBJECT. s.3(5) requires active participation; s.190 requires only membership. s.3(5) applies to any number of persons (two or more); s.190 needs five or more. s.3(5) is about a criminal act; s.190 about an offence committed by any member.

Mere membership is not enough for s.190 if the member joined without sharing the object; innocent bystanders and passers-by are not liable (Masalti v State of UP, 1965). Where a large crowd is named but only a few are proved to be actively involved, courts require that at least five be proved members.

Related new offences: s.196 (promoting enmity between groups; IPC 153A), s.197 (imputations prejudicial to national integration; IPC 153B), s.192 (wantonly giving provocation with intent to cause riot; IPC 153), s.194 (affray, IPC 159-160).

case_laws.case: Barendra Kumar Ghosh v King Emperor (1925)
case_laws.principle: Participation need not be in the commission of the act; standing and waiting (sentry) is participation.

case_laws.case: Mahbub Shah v King-Emperor (1945)
case_laws.principle: Common intention needs a prior meeting of minds; distinct from similar intention.

case_laws.case: Pandurang v State of Hyderabad (1955)
case_laws.principle: Common intention may develop at the spot but must precede the act; prior concert shown by circumstances.

case_laws.case: Krishna Govind Patil v State of Maharashtra (1964)
case_laws.principle: Section 34 applies only if common intention shown; where doubts exist, benefit goes to the accused.

case_laws.case: Masalti v State of UP (1965)
case_laws.principle: Where a large number of persons are accused, conviction under s.149 requires at least five proved to be members; the court should be cautious.

case_laws.case: Lalji v State of UP (1989)
case_laws.principle: Common object: liability under s.149 attaches to all members for offences likely in prosecution of the object; membership is a matter of fact.

exam_traps: Section 3(5)/34 = common intention (any number from two); Section 190/149 = common object (five or more).
Mere presence at the scene does not make one liable under s.34, but in s.149 a member continues to be liable even if he did not actually commit the offence.
Section 34 does not create a separate offence; s.149 does not either, but s.189/191 (unlawful assembly/rioting) do.

mcqs.q: Common intention under s.34 IPC (BNS 3(5)) does NOT require:
mcqs.explain: Two or more persons suffice for common intention; five or more is the requirement for an unlawful assembly.

mcqs.q: 'They also serve who only stand and wait' is associated with which case?
mcqs.explain: Barendra Kumar Ghosh (1925) on participation under s.34.

mcqs.q: An unlawful assembly under BNS requires a minimum of:
mcqs.explain: BNS 189 (IPC 141) requires five or more persons.

ipc_bns_sections.title: Abetment, Criminal Conspiracy and Attempt (BNS ss.45-62)
key_points: Abetment (s.45; IPC 107): a person abets by (1) instigation, (2) engaging in a conspiracy (with an act or illegal omission in pursuance), (3) intentional aiding by act or illegal omission. Explanations: wilful misrepresentation or wilful concealment of a material fact is instigation; facilitating commission of the act counts as aiding.

Abettor (s.46): one who abets an offence or who abets the doing of an act that would be an offence if done by a person capable of law or with the same intent/knowledge. Abetment of abetment is also an offence. Abetment is complete even if the act abetted is not committed.
Punishment (s.49; IPC 109): where the act abetted is committed in consequence and no express provision exists, the abettor gets the same punishment as for the offence.
Abettor present when offence is committed (s.54; IPC 114) is deemed to have committed the offence.
Abetment of offence punishable with death or life imprisonment (s.55; IPC 115): 7 years and fine if the offence is not committed; 14 years if hurt caused.
Abetment of offence punishable with imprisonment (s.56; IPC 116): one-fourth of the longest term (half if the abettor is a public servant).
Abetment by public (s.57; IPC 117): abetting commission of an offence by the public generally or by more than ten persons: imprisonment up to 3 years, fine, or both.
Concealing design to commit offence punishable with death/life (s.58) and by public servant (s.59) (IPC 118, 119).

Criminal conspiracy (s.61; IPC 120A-120B): agreement between two or more persons to do an illegal act or a legal act by illegal means. For agreement to commit an offence, no overt act is needed (except where the agreement is to do an illegal act that is not an offence; then an overt act is required). Punishment: same as abetment for serious offences; 6 months for other conspiracies.

Conspiracy cases: Kehar Singh v State (Delhi Admin), 1988: conspiracy is rarely proved by direct evidence; inference from circumstances. Ram Narain Poply v CBI (2003): conspiracy is a continuing offence. State v Nalini (Rajiv Gandhi assassination, 1999): the court explained how acts of conspirators are admissible under the Evidence Act s.10 (BSA s.8). R. Venkatkrishnan v CBI (2009): mere knowledge is not agreement.

Attempt (s.62; IPC 511): attempt to commit offences punishable with imprisonment (including life): up to half of the longest term for the offence, or the prescribed fine, or both. General attempt provision applies only where no specific attempt provision exists (e.g., attempt to murder in s.109).

Tests of attempt: proximity test (Eagleton, 1855): last act necessary for the offence; locus poenitentiae; Indian courts follow the 'substantial step' or 'unequivocal act' approach. Om Prakash v State of Punjab (1961): attempt begins when preparation is complete and the person commences the actual act. State of Maharashtra v Mohd. Yakub (1980): carrying silver in a truck near the sea at night, held to be attempt to smuggle. Malkiat Singh v State of Punjab (1991): carrying paddy to the border in a truck is preparation, not attempt. Abhayanand Mishra: false application and attempt to cheat.
Impossibility: attempt is punishable even if the act was impossible (pick-pocket with empty pocket: attempt to commit theft). Illustration under BNS 62 / s.511 IPC.

Abetment of suicide: s.108 (IPC 306): up to 10 years and fine. s.107: abetment of suicide of a child or person of unsound mind: death or life or not less than 10 years. Explanations: need for active act of instigation (Gurcharan Singh v State of Punjab, 2020; Chitresh Kumar Chopra v State (NCT of Delhi), 2009; Amalendu Pal v State of WB, 2010; M. Arjunan v State, 2019). Mere harassment or insult is not instigation unless there is mens rea to push the person to suicide. Recent focus: Supreme Court insistence on proximity and clear mens rea, avoiding mechanical invocation (e.g., Mahendra Awase v State of MP, 2025) [VERIFY].

case_laws.case: Kehar Singh v State (Delhi Admin) (1988)
case_laws.principle: Conspiracy: agreement is the gist; proof may be circumstantial; the conspiracy continues as long as the object is not achieved.

case_laws.case: State v Nalini (1999)
case_laws.principle: Rajiv Gandhi assassination: Evidence Act s.10 and the rule of agency in conspiracy.

case_laws.case: Abhayanand Mishra v State of Bihar (1961)
case_laws.principle: Attempt starts when preparation is complete and the first step is taken.

case_laws.case: Malkiat Singh v State of Punjab (1991)
case_laws.principle: Mere carrying of goods towards the border is preparation, not attempt.

case_laws.case: Aman Kumar v State of Haryana (2004)
case_laws.principle: Attempt to murder: an overt act showing proximity to the offence is required; injury is not necessary.

case_laws.case: Gian Kaur v State of Punjab (1996)
case_laws.principle: Right to life does not include right to die; abetment of suicide (and attempt, under then s.309) is constitutionally valid.

case_laws.case: Ramesh Kumar v State of Chhattisgarh (2001)
case_laws.principle: Instigation means to goad, urge forward, provoke or incite; wilful act required.

case_laws.case: Sanju @ Sanjay Singh Sengar v State of MP (2002)
case_laws.principle: A quarrel in which the accused said 'go and die' is not abetment without intention to bring about death.

exam_traps: Abetment of suicide requires positive instigation; harassment alone or one remark in a quarrel is insufficient.
Attempt to suicide (IPC 309) no longer an offence in BNS, except the narrow BNS 226 (to compel or restrain public servant).
Conspiracy requires two or more persons; one cannot conspire alone, and a spouse-only conspiracy remains debated; courts accept that the two must be separately capable.
Specific attempt provisions (s.109 attempt to murder; s.110 attempt to commit culpable homicide) override the general s.62.

mcqs.q: Punishment for abetment of suicide under BNS s.108 is:
mcqs.explain: BNS 108 (IPC 306): imprisonment up to ten years and fine.

mcqs.q: Criminal conspiracy is dealt with in BNS under:
mcqs.explain: BNS 61 (IPC 120A-120B). s.62 is attempt.

mcqs.q: Which case held that the right to life does not include the right to die?
mcqs.explain: Gian Kaur (1996) overruled Rathinam.

ipc_bns_sections.title: Culpable Homicide, Murder, Death by Negligence, Hit and Run, Mob Lynching, Organised Crime
key_points: Culpable homicide (BNS 100; IPC 299): causing death by an act done (a) with the intention of causing death, or (b) with the intention of causing such bodily injury as is likely to cause death, or (c) with the knowledge that the act is likely to cause death.

Murder (BNS 101; IPC 300): culpable homicide is murder if the act is done (1) with intention of causing death; (2) with intention of causing bodily injury the offender knows likely to cause death of the person harmed; (3) with intention of causing bodily injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death; (4) with knowledge that the act is so imminently dangerous that it must in all probability cause death or such injury, and without any excuse for incurring the risk.

Exceptions to murder (culpable homicide not amounting to murder): (1) grave and sudden provocation; (2) exceeding the right of private defence in good faith; (3) public servant exceeding powers for public good; (4) sudden fight in the heat of passion without premeditation and without undue advantage or cruelty; (5) consent of the victim above 18 years.

Provocation tests (Nanavati, 1962): the provocation must be grave and sudden; the reasonable man would be so provoked; the accused must have been deprived of self-control; no time to cool down; the act must be done under the heat of passion. Nanavati: killing paramour after cooling time was murder; the Governor's pardon and jury system are historical notes.

Difference between s.100 (culpable homicide) and s.101 (murder): degree of probability of death. Culpable homicide is the genus and murder the species (Reg v Govinda; State of AP v R. Punnayya, 1976). Clause (3) of s.300 (Virsa Singh v State of Punjab, 1958): injury intended + sufficient in ordinary course of nature to cause death: objective inquiry; accused need not know the injury would be fatal.
Transferred malice (s.101 illustration; IPC 301 = BNS 102): if A intends to kill B but kills C, A is liable as if he had killed B (culpable homicide and murder principles apply).

Punishment for murder (s.103(1)): death or imprisonment for life and fine. s.103(2) is NEW: when a group of five or more persons acting in concert commits murder on the ground of race, caste or community, sex, place of birth, language, personal belief or any other similar ground, each member shall be punished with death or imprisonment for life and also fine, which is the statutory mob lynching offence.

Murder by life convict (IPC 303, mandatory death) was struck down in Mithu v State of Punjab (1983); BNS s.104 (murder by a person already under sentence of imprisonment for life) is punishable with death or imprisonment for life meaning the remainder of natural life; the mandatory death sentence of IPC 303 is not retained [VERIFY wording].

Culpable homicide not amounting to murder (s.105; IPC 304): Part I (intent/knowledge of likely death): imprisonment for life or up to 10 years plus fine. Part II (knowledge without intention): imprisonment up to 10 years, or fine, or both. BNS 105 retains the structure; minimum term unchanged [VERIFY].

Dowry death (s.80(2); IPC 304B): death of a woman within seven years of marriage by burns/bodily injury or otherwise than under normal circumstances, and soon before death subjected to cruelty or harassment by husband or relatives for dowry. Punishment: imprisonment not less than 7 years, may extend to life. Presumption under BSA s.118 (Evidence Act 113B). Key case: Kans Raj v State of Punjab (2000): 'soon before' means proximate and live link; Satbir Singh v State of Haryana (2021): the presumption under Evidence Act applies; courts must read ss.304B and 498A together. Cruelty + dowry demand is the essence.

Causing death by negligence (s.106(1); IPC 304A): up to 5 years plus fine; for registered medical practitioners performing a medical procedure up to 2 years plus fine. Jacob Mathew v State of Punjab (2005): gross negligence or recklessness is required for doctors; simple lack of care insufficient.

Hit and run (s.106(2)): causing death by rash and negligent driving not amounting to culpable homicide and escaping without reporting to police or magistrate soon after: up to 10 years and fine. The provision generated nationwide transporter protests; its operation was held in abeyance pending notification [VERIFY current status].

Abetment of suicide: s.107, s.108 (see 4.4). Attempt to murder (s.109; IPC 307): up to 10 years and fine; if hurt is caused, life or up to 10 years; life convict attempting murder: death or life (s.109(2)). Attempt to commit culpable homicide (s.110; IPC 308): up to 3 years or fine; with hurt up to 7 years.

Organised crime (s.111, new): continuing unlawful activity (kidnapping, robbery, vehicle theft, extortion, land grabbing, contract killing, economic offences, cyber crimes, trafficking of persons, drugs, weapons, illicit goods or services, human trafficking for prostitution or ransom) by a member of an organised crime syndicate, singly or jointly, by use of violence, threat, intimidation, coercion, or other unlawful means to obtain direct or indirect material benefit including financial benefit. Punishment: if it results in death, death or life and fine not less than Rs 10 lakh; otherwise 5 years to life and fine not less than Rs 5 lakh. Members, harbouring, possession of property derived from organised crime, abetment are also punished.

Petty organised crime (s.112): 1 to 7 years and fine for acts by gang such as theft, snatching, cheating, unauthorised selling of tickets, unauthorised betting or gambling, selling public examination question papers.

Terrorist act (s.113): act with intent to threaten unity, integrity, security or economic security of India, or strike terror in people, using bombs, dynamite, explosives, firearms, or other lethal substances; causing death: death or life imprisonment and fine; otherwise 5 years to life and fine. Overlaps with UAPA; the Sanhita attracts the 'which law to apply' discretion of a police officer of rank of SP.

Rarest of rare doctrine: Bachan Singh v State of Punjab (1980) upheld constitutionality of death penalty subject to special reasons (s.354(3) CrPC, BNSS 393(3)); Machhi Singh v State of Punjab (1983) classified categories; Mukesh v State (NCT Delhi) (2017) Nirbhaya; recent emphasis on mitigating factors and sentencing hearing (Manoj v State of MP, 2022); Shatrughan Chauhan (2014) delay in mercy petitions.

case_laws.case: Virsa Singh v State of Punjab (1958)
case_laws.principle: Four-fold test for s.300 clause 3 (now BNS 101(c)): (i) injury present; (ii) injury of the kind intended; (iii) sufficient in ordinary course to cause death; (iv) injury inflicted was intended.

case_laws.case: K.M. Nanavati v State of Maharashtra (1962)
case_laws.principle: Grave and sudden provocation requires the reasonable man test, and the cooling-time test; discussed alongside the jury trial system.

case_laws.case: State of Andhra Pradesh v R. Punnayya (1976)
case_laws.principle: Method for distinguishing culpable homicide and murder: determine whether it is culpable homicide, then whether any clause of s.300 applies.

case_laws.case: Bachan Singh v State of Punjab (1980)
case_laws.principle: Death penalty constitutional; applied only in the rarest of rare cases after balancing aggravating and mitigating circumstances.

case_laws.case: Machhi Singh v State of Punjab (1983)
case_laws.principle: Categories of rarest of rare: manner of commission, motive, anti-social nature, magnitude, personality of victim.

case_laws.case: Mithu v State of Punjab (1983)
case_laws.principle: Mandatory death sentence under IPC 303 violates Articles 14 and 21.

case_laws.case: Jacob Mathew v State of Punjab (2005)
case_laws.principle: Gross negligence (not ordinary) is needed for criminal liability of professionals; guidelines on prosecution of doctors.

case_laws.case: Alister Anthony Pareira v State of Maharashtra (2012)
case_laws.principle: Drunken driving causing deaths: s.304A vs 304 Part II; knowledge may be inferred where driving was grossly reckless.

case_laws.case: Kans Raj v State of Punjab (2000)
case_laws.principle: 'Soon before her death' requires a proximate and live link between cruelty and death.

case_laws.case: Satbir Singh v State of Haryana (2021)
case_laws.principle: Dowry death: presumption under s.113B and interplay of ss.304B and 498A.

case_laws.case: Reg v Govinda (1876)
case_laws.principle: Distinction between culpable homicide and murder; intention to cause a bodily injury likely to cause death.

case_laws.case: Mukesh v State (NCT of Delhi) (2017)
case_laws.principle: Death penalty for Nirbhaya gang-rape and murder, rarest of rare.

exam_traps: Murder = culpable homicide + one of four clauses; not every death by intent is murder if an exception applies.
The five Exceptions are tested directly: provocation, private defence excess, public servant, sudden fight, consent.
Section 304A (negligence) is outside the s.100 to 101 family; it covers rash or negligent acts that do not amount to culpable homicide.
Mob lynching: five or more persons, listed grounds, punishment death or life (BNS 103(2)); students confuse it with unlawful assembly rioting.
Dowry death minimum is 7 years; punishment may go to life.
Organised crime fine minimum: Rs 10 lakh if death; Rs 5 lakh otherwise.

mcqs.q: BNS section that punishes murder is:
mcqs.explain: s.101 defines murder, s.103 prescribes punishment, s.100 defines culpable homicide, s.105 punishes culpable homicide not amounting to murder.

mcqs.q: The minimum punishment for dowry death is:
mcqs.explain: BNS 80(2) (IPC 304B): not less than 7 years, which may extend to life.

mcqs.q: Mob lynching under BNS requires a group of at least:
mcqs.explain: BNS 103(2): a group of five or more persons.

mcqs.q: The 'rarest of rare' doctrine was laid down in:
mcqs.explain: Bachan Singh (1980); Machhi Singh gave categories.

mcqs.q: Which of these is NOT an exception to murder?
mcqs.explain: Necessity is a general exception (s.19), not an exception to murder in s.101.

ipc_bns_sections.title: Hurt, Grievous Hurt, Acid Attack, Wrongful Restraint/Confinement, Force, Assault
key_points: Hurt (s.114; IPC 319): causing bodily pain, disease or infirmity. Voluntarily causing hurt (s.115(2); IPC 323): up to 1 year or fine up to Rs 10,000 or both.

Grievous hurt (s.116; IPC 320) eight kinds: emasculation; permanent privation of sight of either eye; permanent privation of hearing of either ear; privation of any member or joint; destruction or permanent impairing of powers of any member or joint; permanent disfiguration of the head or face; fracture or dislocation of a bone or tooth; any hurt which endangers life or causes severe bodily pain for 20 days or renders the sufferer unable to follow ordinary pursuits for 20 days.

Voluntarily causing grievous hurt (s.117(2); IPC 325): up to 7 years and fine. BNS 117(3): where hurt results in permanent disability or persistent vegetative state: rigorous imprisonment not less than 10 years, which may extend to life [VERIFY]. BNS 117(4): group of five or more on grounds of race, caste, etc.: up to 7 years and fine (mob-lynching-type for grievous hurt).
Hurt by dangerous weapons (s.118; IPC 324, 326): hurt by weapon or means likely to cause death: up to 3 years; grievous hurt by such means: life or up to 10 years.

Acid attack (s.124; IPC 326A, 326B): causing permanent or partial damage or deformity by acid: not less than 10 years extendable to life, with fine payable to victim to meet medical expenses; throwing or attempting to throw acid: 5 to 7 years and fine. Laxmi v Union of India (2014): regulation of acid sales and compensation.
Hurt to extort property or to constrain an illegal act: ss.119; to extort confession: s.120; to deter public servant: s.121; by poison to commit an offence: s.123.
Act endangering life or personal safety of others (s.125; IPC 336-338).

Wrongful restraint (s.126; IPC 339): obstructing a person from proceeding in a direction in which he has a right to proceed; up to 1 month or fine Rs 5,000 or both. Wrongful confinement (s.127; IPC 340): restraint so as to prevent proceeding beyond limits; 1 year or Rs 5,000 fine; confinement for 3 days or more: up to 2 years; confinement in secret: more.

Force (s.128) and criminal force (s.129; IPC 350): intentional use of force without consent to commit an offence or cause injury, fear or annoyance. Assault (s.130; IPC 351): gesture or preparation causing apprehension of criminal force; mere words do not amount to assault unless accompanied by gestures. Punishment s.131: up to 3 months or fine Rs 1,000 or both.

Assault or criminal force to deter a public servant from duty (s.132; IPC 353): up to 2 years or fine or both. Assault with intent to dishonour (s.133; IPC 355): up to 2 years. Assault in attempt to commit theft (s.134); attempt wrongfully to confine (s.135); grave provocation (s.136) [VERIFY numbering of ss.132-136 against the bare act].
Grievous hurt differs from hurt by degree and by the closed list in s.116; the tests are 'permanent' and '20 days'.
Related: kidnapping and abduction (below, 4.7).
exam_traps: 'Grievous hurt' list is exhaustive (eight kinds); fracture or dislocation of a bone or tooth counts even if it heals.
20-day rule: severe bodily pain or inability to follow ordinary pursuits for 20 days.
Mere words never amount to assault; a gesture plus apprehension is required.
Acid attack minimum: 10 years; throwing/attempt: 5 to 7 years.

mcqs.q: Fracture of a bone or tooth is:
mcqs.explain: Fracture or dislocation of a bone or tooth is the seventh kind of grievous hurt (BNS 116).

mcqs.q: Minimum imprisonment for causing hurt by acid under BNS 124(1) is:
mcqs.explain: Not less than 10 years, may extend to life, with fine.

mcqs.q: Mere words, without gesture, amount to:
mcqs.explain: Explanation to assault: mere words do not amount to assault.

ipc_bns_sections.title: Offences against Women and Children (Chapter V): Rape, Sexual Harassment, Stalking, Voyeurism, Cruelty, Kidnapping, Trafficking
key_points: Rape (s.63; IPC 375): sexual intercourse (penetration of the vagina, mouth, urethra or anus in any manner; application of mouth) by a man with a woman under seven descriptions: against her will; without her consent; consent obtained by putting her or any person in whom she is interested in fear of death or hurt; consent given believing the man to be her husband; consent given by a person of unsound mind or intoxicated or administered stupefying substance; with or without consent when under 18 years; when unable to communicate consent.

Consent: unequivocal voluntary agreement by words, gestures or any form of non-verbal communication; mere absence of resistance is not consent. Exceptions: (1) medical procedure; (2) sexual intercourse by a man with his own wife, wife not being under 18 years, is not rape (Exception 2; Independent Thought v UoI, 2017 read down the age to 18). The marital rape exception is under constitutional challenge before the Supreme Court [VERIFY current status].

Punishment (s.64): rigorous imprisonment not less than 10 years, may extend to life, and fine. Aggravated rape (s.64(2)): by police officer, public servant, armed forces member, jail/remand home staff, hospital staff, relative/guardian/teacher, communal or sectarian violence, pregnant woman, woman incapable of giving consent, one in control or dominance, disabled woman, repeated rape of same woman, grievous bodily harm/maim/disfigure/endanger life: not less than 10 years, may extend to imprisonment for life meaning remainder of natural life, and fine.

Rape of a woman under 16 (s.65(1)): not less than 20 years, may extend to life (remainder of natural life) and fine; under 12 (s.65(2)): not less than 20 years, life (remainder of natural life) or death.
Rape causing death or persistent vegetative state (s.66): not less than 20 years, may extend to life (natural life) or death. Repeat offenders (s.71): life (natural life) or death.
Gang rape (s.70): 20 years to life (natural life) and fine payable to the victim; gang rape of a woman under 18: life (natural life) or death.
Sexual intercourse by husband upon wife during judicial separation (s.67): 2 to 7 years and fine. Sexual intercourse by person in authority (s.68): 5 to 10 years and fine.

Sexual intercourse by deceitful means or false promise of marriage (s.69, NEW): up to 10 years and fine; 'deceitful means' includes inducement for employment/promotion, false identity and false promise to marry without intention to fulfil. Supreme Court earlier distinguished false promise from breach of promise: Uday v State of Karnataka (2003); Pramod Suryabhan Pawar v State of Maharashtra (2019); Anurag Soni v State of Chhattisgarh (2019).

Identity of victim (s.72; IPC 228A): disclosure punishable with up to 2 years and fine; s.73: printing or publishing court proceedings without permission, up to 2 years and fine. Nipun Saxena v UoI (2018) on non-disclosure of identity; the victim's name may not be disclosed even in judgments.

Assault or criminal force to a woman with intent to outrage her modesty (s.74; IPC 354): 1 to 5 years and fine. Test of modesty: Rupan Deol Bajaj v KPS Gill (1995); State of Punjab v Major Singh (1967): the act must offend the sense of decency of a woman.

Sexual harassment (s.75; IPC 354A): physical contact and advances involving unwelcome and explicit sexual overtures; demand or request for sexual favours; showing pornography against will; sexually coloured remarks. Punishment: up to 3 years (first three kinds) or up to 1 year (remarks) and fine.

Assault with intent to disrobe (s.76; IPC 354B): 3 to 7 years and fine. Voyeurism (s.77; IPC 354C): watching or capturing image of a woman in a private act; 1 to 3 years on first conviction, 3 to 7 years on repeat.

Stalking (s.78; IPC 354D): following or contacting a woman despite clear indication of disinterest; monitoring internet, email or electronic communication; first conviction up to 3 years and fine, second 5 years. Exceptions: for preventing or detecting crime authorised by the State; under law; reasonable and justified.
Word, gesture or act intended to insult the modesty of a woman (s.79; IPC 509): up to 3 years and fine.

Cruelty by husband or relatives (s.85; IPC 498A): up to 3 years and fine. 'Cruelty' (s.86): wilful conduct likely to drive the woman to suicide or cause grave injury/danger to life, limb or health (mental or physical); harassment to coerce her or her relatives to meet unlawful demand for property or valuable security. Supreme Court cautions against implicating the entire family without specific allegations: Arnesh Kumar v State of Bihar (2014) (no automatic arrest); Preeti Gupta v State of Jharkhand (2010); Kahkashan Kausar v State of Bihar (2022); Achin Gupta v State of Haryana (2024) [VERIFY]. Rajesh Sharma (2017) guidelines on Family Welfare Committees were modified in Social Action Forum for Manav Adhikar v UoI (2018).

Bigamy (s.82; IPC 494): marrying again during the life of spouse: up to 7 years and fine; concealment of former marriage: up to 10 years. Sarla Mudgal v UoI (1995): conversion to Islam for second marriage does not dissolve the first; bigamy punishable.

Adultery (IPC 497) was struck down in Joseph Shine v UoI (2018) and is not in BNS; no corresponding provision. IPC 377 (unnatural offences) is not in BNS, but non-consensual carnal intercourse persists in discussions [VERIFY].

Kidnapping (s.137; IPC 359-361): kidnapping from India, or from lawful guardianship (under the IPC: a boy under 16 or a girl under 18; BNS s.137 uses 'child', that is, below 18, for both sexes [VERIFY]; or a person of unsound mind). Abduction (s.138; IPC 362): by force or deceitful means to compel a person to go from any place. Kidnapping from lawful guardianship is complete when the minor is taken or enticed away (it is not a continuing offence, whereas abduction is); S. Varadarajan v State of Madras (1965): the minor must be taken or enticed, not merely voluntarily accompany the accused.

Punishment for kidnapping (s.137(2)): up to 7 years and fine. Kidnapping for ransom (s.140(2); IPC 364A): death or life and fine. Kidnapping in order to murder (s.140(1)): life or rigorous imprisonment up to 10 years. Kidnapping to compel marriage (s.87; IPC 366): not less than 10 years, may extend to life [VERIFY numbers].

Trafficking of persons (s.143; IPC 370): recruiting, transporting, harbouring or receiving persons by threats, force, coercion, abduction, fraud, deception, abuse of power or inducement for exploitation. Punishment: 7 to 10 years; more than one person 10 years to life; minor: 10 years to life; more than one minor: 14 years to life; repeat offender: life (natural life). Exploitation of trafficked person (s.144; IPC 370A): 3 to 5 years (5-7 where a minor). Child-related: procuring (s.96), selling a minor for prostitution (s.98): 10 years to life; buying a minor (s.99): 10 years to life.

Concealment of birth (s.94), causing miscarriage (s.88: up to 3 years; woman: up to 7 years), without consent (s.89: life or up to 10), death by act to cause miscarriage (s.90), act to prevent a child being born alive (s.91), death of quick unborn child (s.92). The MTP Act 1971 (as amended 2021) permits termination up to 24 weeks for specified categories.

Related statutes frequently tested alongside: POCSO Act 2012 (penetrative sexual assault on a child; age of consent 18; mandatory reporting); Criminal Law (Amendment) Act 2013 (Nirbhaya); Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act 2013; Juvenile Justice Act 2015 (heinous offences by 16-18-year-olds may be tried as adults after preliminary assessment, Shilpa Mittal v State of NCT Delhi, 2020).

case_laws.case: Tukaram v State of Maharashtra (Mathura rape case) (1979)
case_laws.principle: Acquittal on 'consent' reasoning led to 1983 amendments: presumption of no consent on proof of sexual intercourse where victim says she did not consent (BSA s.120).

case_laws.case: State of Punjab v Gurmit Singh (1996)
case_laws.principle: Conviction in rape may rest on sole testimony of the prosecutrix; courts must be sensitive; in-camera trials.

case_laws.case: Independent Thought v Union of India (2017)
case_laws.principle: Exception 2 to s.375 read down: sexual intercourse with a wife under 18 is rape.

case_laws.case: Mukesh v State (NCT of Delhi) (2017)
case_laws.principle: Death sentence confirmed for Nirbhaya convicts.

case_laws.case: Vishaka v State of Rajasthan (1997)
case_laws.principle: Guidelines against sexual harassment at workplace; led to the 2013 Act.

case_laws.case: Rupan Deol Bajaj v KPS Gill (1995)
case_laws.principle: Modesty of a woman: the ultimate test is whether the action offends the sense of decency of a woman.

case_laws.case: Sarla Mudgal v Union of India (1995)
case_laws.principle: Second marriage after conversion remains bigamy.

case_laws.case: Joseph Shine v Union of India (2018)
case_laws.principle: Adultery (IPC 497) unconstitutional; women not chattel.

case_laws.case: Arnesh Kumar v State of Bihar (2014)
case_laws.principle: 498A arrests must follow checklist under s.41 CrPC (now BNSS 35); no mechanical arrest.

case_laws.case: Laxmi v Union of India (2014)
case_laws.principle: Acid sale regulation and compensation for acid-attack victims.

case_laws.case: Pramod Suryabhan Pawar v State of Maharashtra (2019)
case_laws.principle: Consent obtained on a false promise of marriage vitiates consent only if the promise was false from inception.

case_laws.case: S. Varadarajan v State of Madras (1965)
case_laws.principle: Taking is not the same as allowing a minor to accompany; kidnapping requires active inducement.

exam_traps: Age of consent for sexual intercourse is 18 years; exception for wife is also 18 (Independent Thought).
False promise of marriage: BNS 69 is now a standalone offence (up to 10 years), distinct from rape.
Stalking, voyeurism and harassment: remember repeat-offender enhancements.
Cruelty under s.85 has two limbs (health/suicide-driving and dowry harassment).
Gang rape of a minor under 18: life (natural life) or death; for adult woman: 20 years to life.
Disclosure of victim's identity is an offence (up to 2 years and fine), including through publication of court records without leave.

mcqs.q: BNS section which defines rape is:
mcqs.explain: s.63 defines rape (IPC 375); s.64 punishes it.

mcqs.q: Sexual intercourse by deceitful means, including false promise of marriage, is punishable under BNS:
mcqs.explain: BNS 69 is a new offence; up to 10 years and fine.

mcqs.q: BNS section corresponding to IPC 498A is:
mcqs.explain: s.85 punishes cruelty; s.86 defines cruelty.

mcqs.q: Dowry death is covered under BNS:
mcqs.explain: BNS 80 (IPC 304B).

mcqs.q: Which judgment struck down adultery as an offence?
mcqs.explain: Joseph Shine v UoI (2018).

ipc_bns_sections.title: Offences against the State, Public Tranquillity, Hate Speech and Religion
key_points: Waging war against the Government of India (s.147; IPC 121): death or life imprisonment and fine. Conspiracy to commit offences against the State (s.148; IPC 121A): life or up to 10 years. Collecting arms to wage war (s.149; IPC 122); concealing a design to wage war (s.150; IPC 123); assaulting the President or Governor with intent to compel or restrain exercise of lawful power (s.151; IPC 124).

Acts endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity of India (s.152; replaces IPC 124A sedition): whoever, purposely or knowingly, by words (spoken or written), signs, visible representation, electronic communication or use of financial means, or otherwise, excites or attempts to excite secession, armed rebellion, subversive activities, encourages feelings of separatist activities, or endangers sovereignty or unity and integrity of India, shall be punished with life imprisonment or imprisonment up to 7 years and fine. Explanation: comments expressing disapprobation of measures of government with a view to obtain their alteration by lawful means do not constitute the offence.

Sedition background: Kedar Nath Singh v State of Bihar (1962) limited s.124A to acts with a tendency to incite violence or public disorder; Balwant Singh v State of Punjab (1995) (slogans); S.G. Vombatkere v UoI (2022): operation of s.124A kept in abeyance; BNS 152 is challenged as retaining sedition in substance [VERIFY pending challenges].

Unlawful assembly (s.189), common object (s.190), rioting (s.191): see 4.3. Punishment for rioting (s.191(2)): up to 2 years or fine or both; rioting armed with a deadly weapon (s.191(3)): up to 5 years; unlawful assembly (s.189(2)): up to 6 months; unlawful assembly armed: up to 2 years.
Affray (s.194; IPC 159-160): two or more persons fighting in a public place disturbing the public peace: up to 1 month or fine Rs 1,000.

Promoting enmity between different groups on grounds of religion, race, place of birth, residence, language, etc. (s.196; IPC 153A): up to 3 years or fine or both; in a place of worship or at religious gatherings, up to 5 years and fine. Section 197 (IPC 153B): imputations and assertions prejudicial to national integration: up to 3 years.

Hate speech jurisprudence: Pravasi Bhalai Sangathan v UoI (2014): Law Commission to examine; Amish Devgan v UoI (2020): speech is judged by the reasonable, strong-minded, firm and courageous person standard, not weak and vacillating minds, and context and intent matter; Arup Bhuyan v State of Assam (2011): mere membership of a banned organisation is not an offence unless the accused incites violence; Shreya Singhal v UoI (2015): discussion and advocacy are protected, incitement is not (Section 66A IT Act struck down); Imran Pratapgadhi v State of Gujarat (2025): speech must be judged by the standards of reasonable, strong-minded persons; creative expression and a poem do not by themselves attract ss.196/197/299 [VERIFY].

Offences relating to religion: injuring or defiling a place of worship (s.298; IPC 295): up to 2 years or fine or both; deliberate and malicious acts intended to outrage religious feelings (s.299; IPC 295A): up to 3 years or fine or both (Ramji Lal Modi v State of UP, 1957 upheld 295A as a reasonable restriction); disturbing religious assembly (s.300); trespassing on burial places (s.301); uttering words with deliberate intent to wound religious feelings (s.302; IPC 298): up to 1 year.

Obstructing public servants and public duty: assaulting or obstructing a public servant when suppressing riot (s.195); obstructing a public servant in discharge of public functions (s.221; IPC 186): up to 3 months or Rs 2,500 fine; disobedience to order duly promulgated by a public servant (s.223; IPC 188): up to 6 months if it causes obstruction; up to 1 year if danger to life, health or safety or riot. Note that s.223 is now a cognizable-complaint structure tied to BNSS s.215 (complaint by the public servant).

Absconding to avoid service of summons is BNS s.206 (IPC 172); non-attendance in obedience to an order from a public servant is s.209 (IPC 174), where community service is an alternative punishment. Giving false information to a public servant (s.217; IPC 182): up to 6 months or fine up to Rs 5,000.

Public servants: taking gratification other than legal remuneration, bribery and other corruption offences: now under the Prevention of Corruption Act 1988 (amended 2018); IPC 161-165A were repealed earlier, and BNS retains only limited provisions (e.g., s.198 public servant disobeying direction under law).

ipc_bns_sections.title: Offences against Property: Theft, Snatching, Extortion, Robbery, Dacoity, Criminal Misappropriation, Criminal Breach of Trust, Cheating, Stolen Property, Mischief, Trespass
key_points: Theft (s.303; IPC 378): dishonestly taking any movable property out of the possession of any person without his consent, moving the property in order to such taking. Ingredients: dishonest intention; movable property; out of possession; without consent; moving. Pyare Lal Bhargava v State of Rajasthan (1963): temporary removal with dishonest intention is theft. K.N. Mehra v State of Rajasthan (1957): taking an aircraft; intention to take dishonestly is satisfied even if the property is to be returned later. Earth attached to the earth becomes movable once severed.

Punishment for theft (s.303(2)): up to 3 years or fine or both; repeat conviction: 1 to 5 years and fine; community service in the case of a first-time offender where the stolen property value is below Rs 5,000 and it is returned or its value restored.

Snatching (s.304, NEW): theft by suddenly or quickly or forcibly seizing or securing or grabbing or taking away from any person or from his possession any movable property, in order to commit theft: up to 3 years and fine.

Theft in a dwelling house, transport, place of worship (s.305): up to 7 years and fine. Theft by clerk or servant (s.306): up to 7 years and fine. Theft after preparation for causing death, hurt or restraint (s.307): up to 10 years rigorous imprisonment.

Extortion (s.308; IPC 383): intentionally putting any person in fear of injury and thereby dishonestly inducing him to deliver property or valuable security. Punishment: up to 7 years or fine or both; putting person in fear of death or grievous hurt: up to 10 years; accusing of an offence punishable with death or life: up to 10 years.

Robbery (s.309; IPC 390): theft or extortion becomes robbery when, in order to committing theft or in committing or carrying away property, the offender voluntarily causes or attempts to cause death, hurt or wrongful restraint, or fear of instant death, instant hurt or instant wrongful restraint. Punishment s.309(4): rigorous imprisonment up to 10 years and fine; highway robbery between sunset and sunrise: up to 14 years.

Dacoity (s.310; IPC 391): five or more persons conjointly commit or attempt to commit robbery, or where the whole number of persons conjointly committing, attempting and aiding amounts to five or more. Punishment: life or rigorous imprisonment up to 10 years and fine. Dacoity with murder: death, life or rigorous imprisonment not less than 10 years (s.310(3)). Robbery or dacoity with attempt to cause death or grievous hurt (s.311): not less than 7 years. Attempt to commit robbery or dacoity when armed (s.312): not less than 7 years. Belonging to a gang of dacoits: life or rigorous imprisonment up to 10 years (BNS 310(4), 310(5)).

Theft vs extortion vs robbery: in theft, property is taken without consent; in extortion, consent is obtained by fear; in robbery, there is theft or extortion plus instant violence or the fear of it. Robbery is the common denominator of both.

Dishonest misappropriation of property (s.314; IPC 403): dishonestly misappropriating or converting to own use any movable property; 6 months to 2 years and fine. Misappropriation of property of a deceased person (s.315; IPC 404): 6 months to 3 years; clerk or servant: up to 7 years. Distinction from theft: in misappropriation the property comes into the accused's possession innocently (finding lost property) and the dishonest intention arises later.

Criminal breach of trust (CBT) (s.316; IPC 405): entrustment with property or dominion over it and dishonest misappropriation or conversion, use or disposal of property in violation of the law or contract. Punishment: s.316(2): up to 5 years or fine or both; s.316(3) carrier, wharfinger or warehouse-keeper: up to 7 years and fine; s.316(4) clerk or servant: up to 7 years and fine; s.316(5) public servant, banker, merchant, agent, broker, attorney: life or up to 10 years and fine. Key cases: R.K. Dalmia v Delhi Administration (1962): 'property' includes funds of a company; Velji Raghavji Patel v State of Maharashtra (1965): a partner is not liable for CBT of partnership property unless a specific entrustment is shown. Entrustment is the key to CBT.

Receiving stolen property (s.317; IPC 410-414): 'stolen property' includes property transferred by theft, extortion, robbery, criminal misappropriation or CBT; dishonestly receiving: up to 3 years (s.317(2)); habitually dealing: life or up to 10 years; assisting in concealment: up to 3 years.

Cheating (s.318; IPC 415): by deceiving a person, fraudulently or dishonestly inducing him to deliver property to any person or consent that any person shall retain any property, or intentionally inducing him to do or omit to do anything which he would not do if not deceived and which causes or is likely to cause damage or harm to body, mind, reputation or property. Punishment: s.318(2) up to 3 years or fine or both; s.318(3) cheating with knowledge that wrongful loss may be caused to a person whose interest the offender is bound to protect: up to 5 years; s.318(4) cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property or making, altering or destroying valuable security: up to 7 years and fine.

Cheating vs CBT vs breach of contract: Hridaya Ranjan Prasad Verma v State of Bihar (2000): to constitute cheating, intention to deceive must exist at the time of making the promise; mere breach of contract does not become cheating. Iridium India Telecom v Motorola (2011): a company may be prosecuted for offences requiring mens rea; corporate criminal liability established. Sunil Bharti Mittal v CBI (2015): directors are not vicariously liable merely because of their post; alter ego doctrine.
Cheating by personation (s.319; IPC 416): up to 5 years or fine; Fraudulent removal or concealment of property (s.320-322 etc.).

Mischief (s.324; IPC 425): intent or knowledge of causing wrongful loss or damage to the public or to any person, and causing the destruction of any property or any change in it or its situation which destroys or diminishes its value or utility. Punishment is graded by the amount of damage and the means used (for example, mischief by fire or explosive substance is punished far more severely); check the thresholds in s.324 of the bare act [VERIFY].

Criminal trespass (s.329(1); IPC 441): entry into or upon property in possession of another with intent to commit an offence or to intimidate, insult or annoy; or unlawfully remaining. Punishment: up to 3 months or fine up to Rs 5,000; house trespass (s.329(3)): up to 1 year or fine up to Rs 5,000; lurking house trespass and house-breaking (ss.330-331): housebreaking: up to 2 years; house-breaking by night: up to 3 years; lurking house-trespass and house-breaking in order to commit an offence punishable with death/imprisonment: 10 years etc. [VERIFY exact numbering of 330-334].

Forgery and documents: Forgery (s.336; IPC 463): making a false document or electronic record with intent to cause damage or injury to the public or any person, or to support any claim or title, or to cause any person to part with property, or to enter into an express or implied contract, or with intent to commit fraud or that fraud may be committed. Punishment (s.336(2)): up to 2 years or fine or both; forgery for cheating (s.336(3)): up to 7 years and fine; forgery to harm reputation (s.336(4)): up to 3 years and fine. Making a false document is defined in s.335; using as genuine a forged document: s.340. Mohd Ibrahim v State of Bihar (2009): a person who sells a property he does not own does not commit forgery by executing a sale deed in his own name; false document requires that the document purports to be someone else's.
Falsification of accounts (s.344; IPC 477A): up to 7 years or fine or both. Counterfeiting coins and currency notes: ss.178-188 (IPC 231-263A) [VERIFY].
Hot topics: cyber and digital cheating via electronic records and the new definition of 'document'; organised crime provisions covering economic offences; theft of vehicles linked to organised crime.

ipc_bns_sections.title: Defamation, Criminal Intimidation, Insult, Obscenity, Public Nuisance, False Evidence, Public Health and Safety

refs.bns: Ss. 227-269 (false evidence and justice), 270-297 (public health and decency), 351-357

key_points: Defamation (s.356; IPC 499): making or publishing any imputation concerning any person intending to harm, or knowing or having reason to believe that such imputation will harm, the reputation of such person, by words spoken or intended to be read, signs, visible representations or electronic means. Punishment (s.356(2)): simple imprisonment up to 2 years, or fine, or both, or community service. Ten exceptions: truth for public good; public conduct of public servants; conduct of any person touching public question; reports of court proceedings; merits of a case decided by court or witnesses and conduct; merits of public performance; censure by authority; accusation in good faith to authorised person; imputation by a person on his own character for protection of interest; caution intended for the good of the person or for public good.

Criminal defamation constitutional: Subramanian Swamy v UoI (2016) upheld IPC 499-500 as a reasonable restriction under Article 19(2) protecting reputation as part of Article 21. Defamation of the deceased, of a company or collection of persons is possible if the imputation would harm the reputation if living.
Printing or engraving defamatory matter; sale of printed defamatory matter (s.357): up to 2 years.

Criminal intimidation (s.351; IPC 503): threatening a person with injury to person, reputation or property, or to any person in whom he is interested, with intent to cause alarm or to cause him to do any act he is not legally bound to do. Punishment s.351(2): up to 2 years or fine or both; threat of death or grievous hurt, imputation of unchastity to a woman, etc. (s.351(3)): up to 7 years; anonymous communication (s.351(4)): up to 2 years additional. Criminal intimidation by anonymous communication is aggravated.

Intentional insult with intent to provoke breach of the peace (s.352; IPC 504): up to 2 years or fine or both. Statements conducing to public mischief (s.353; IPC 505): up to 3 years; rumour or false information spreading alarm (including by electronic means), or inciting groups: up to 3 years; in a place of worship: up to 5 years.
Misconduct in public by a drunken person (s.355; IPC 510): up to 24 hours simple imprisonment or fine up to Rs 1,000 or community service.

Obscenity (s.294; IPC 292): obscene if lascivious or appeals to prurient interest or tends to deprave and corrupt persons likely to read, see or hear it. Test: Hicklin test (adopted in Ranjit Udeshi v State of Maharashtra, 1965) replaced by the community standards test in Aveek Sarkar v State of West Bengal (2014) and Bobby Art International v Om Pal Singh Hoon (1996, Bandit Queen). Punishment: first conviction up to 2 years and fine up to Rs 5,000; subsequent conviction up to 5 years and fine up to Rs 10,000. Sale of obscene objects to a child (s.295): 3 years first, 7 years later. Obscene acts and songs in public (s.296): up to 3 months or fine Rs 1,000. Overlap with IT Act 2000 ss.67-67B.

Public nuisance (s.270; IPC 268): an act or illegal omission causing common injury, danger or annoyance to the public or to people in general in the vicinity. Punishment (s.292): fine up to Rs 1,000; community service possible. Negligent act likely to spread infection of disease dangerous to life (s.271; IPC 269): up to 6 months or fine; malignant act (s.272; IPC 270): up to 2 years.

Adulteration of food or drink intended for sale (s.274; IPC 272): up to 6 months and fine up to Rs 5,000; sale of noxious food or drink (s.275; IPC 273): same; adulteration or sale of drugs (ss.276-278): 6 months to 1 year etc. Rash driving or riding on a public way (s.281; IPC 279): up to 6 months or fine up to Rs 1,000. Rash navigation of a vessel (s.282). Negligent conduct with respect to poisonous substances, fire, explosive substances, machinery, building collapse, animals (ss.286-291).

False evidence (s.227; IPC 191): being legally bound by oath or express provision of law to state the truth, or bound by law to make a declaration, makes a statement which is false and which he either knows or believes to be false or does not believe to be true. Punishment for false evidence (s.229(1); IPC 193): up to 7 years and fine in judicial proceedings; up to 3 years in other cases. Fabricating false evidence (s.228, 230): up to 7 years, or life if used to procure conviction for a capital offence. Giving or fabricating false evidence with intent to procure conviction of a capital offence: life or rigorous up to 10 years; if an innocent person is executed: death or the above.

Section 195 CrPC (BNSS 215) bars courts from taking cognizance of ss.172-188 (contempt of lawful authority) and offences against public justice (ss.193-229) except on a written complaint by the court or public servant concerned. Perjury offences require a complaint by the court; Iqbal Singh Marwah v Meenakshi Marwah (2005) on forged documents and s.195 CrPC.

Causing disappearance of evidence of an offence or giving false information to screen the offender (s.238; IPC 201): punishment depends on the gravity of the offence screened: 7 years if offence punishable with death; 3 years if punishable with life or up to 10 years; one-fourth in other cases.

False charge of offence made with intent to injure (s.248; IPC 211): up to 2 years or fine or both; if the charge is of an offence punishable with death, life or 7 years or more: up to 7 years and fine. Harbouring offender: s.249-252.

Contempt of lawful authority (Chapter XIV): non-attendance in obedience to summons (s.209) and community service; obstruction (s.221); threatening a public servant (s.224); refusing to be sworn (s.229-like); omission to assist public servant (s.222 etc.) [VERIFY section numbers].

ipc_bns_sections.title: Transition from IPC to BNS: Temporal Application, Savings and Constitutional Limits
key_points: Three new codes replaced the colonial criminal law with effect from 1 July 2024: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) replaced the Indian Penal Code, 1860; Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) replaced the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973; Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) replaced the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. Each received Presidential assent on 25 December 2023.

Rule of temporal application: BNS applies to offences committed on or after 1 July 2024. Offences committed before that date continue to be governed by the IPC, even if the FIR is registered, or the trial takes place, after that date. This follows Article 20(1) of the Constitution: no person shall be convicted of any offence except for violation of a law in force at the time of the commission of the act, nor subjected to a penalty greater than that which might have been inflicted under the law in force at the time.

Article 20(1) bars ex post facto CRIMINAL LAWS and enhanced penalties; it does not bar retrospective procedural changes. The beneficial-provision principle: where the new law reduces the punishment, the accused may claim the benefit of the lighter punishment (T. Barai v Henry Ah Hoe, 1983; Rattan Lal v State of Punjab, 1964: benefit of ameliorative provisions).

Procedure for pending matters: BNSS s.531 (repeal and savings) provides that pending appeals, applications, trials, inquiries and investigations under the CrPC continue under the CrPC as if it had not been repealed. A trial that began before 1 July 2024 continues under the CrPC; a fresh FIR for an offence committed before that date is registered under the BNSS procedure but the substantive offence is the IPC offence.

Continuing offences and offences spanning the cut-off date: where the commission of the offence began before 1 July 2024 and continued after, courts look at the date on which the offence is complete; for a continuing offence, the law in force when the conduct continues applies to the post-cut-off conduct. The Supreme Court and High Courts have stressed that the FIR must correctly invoke the Code in force on the date of the alleged offence; invoking the wrong Code is generally a curable defect unless it causes prejudice [VERIFY the latest judgments].

BNS has 358 sections in 20 chapters (IPC: 511 sections in 23 chapters). Official summaries speak of about 20 new offences and about 19 repealed provisions; remember the broad picture rather than exact counts [VERIFY].

Savings clause (BNS s.358): repeals the IPC but preserves the effect of the repealed Code on offences committed before commencement, and any notification, rules or orders made under the IPC are saved to the extent consistent with the BNS.

Special and local laws: the general provisions of the Code (definitions, general exceptions, abetment and so on) apply to offences under special and local laws unless excluded, and the Code does not affect special or local laws (IPC s.5 saving, carried into the BNS preliminary provisions) [VERIFY exact BNS section].

Territorial scope: the Code operates over every person for acts or omissions within India; for citizens and for ships/aircraft registered in India; for offences by any person targeting a computer resource in India. Section 1(5): the BNS applies to any offence committed by a citizen of India outside India, to any person on a ship or aircraft registered in India wherever it may be, to any person outside India who commits an offence targeting a computer resource located in India. [VERIFY the exact wording of s.1(5) in the bare act].

Explanation of s.1: the word 'offence' includes every act committed outside India which, if committed in India, would be punishable under the Code. Extradition and trial in India: BNSS s.208 (CrPC 188) requires sanction of the Central Government for inquiry or trial of an offence committed abroad by a citizen.

Persons exempt from the operation of the Code: the President and Governors (Art. 361: no criminal proceedings during term of office), foreign sovereigns and ambassadors (diplomatic immunity under the Diplomatic Relations (Vienna Convention) Act, 1972), foreign armies with consent, and Members of Parliament/Legislatures for privileged statements (Arts. 105, 194).

Hot exam point: the new codes dropped the word 'Indian' in favour of 'Bharatiya', and the substance of many IPC provisions was carried verbatim. Where the exam asks 'under which Code would X be tried', first check the date of the offence.

Offences under special laws (NDPS, PMLA, UAPA, POCSO, IT Act, PC Act) are not affected by the repeal of the IPC, except where the special law cross-refers to IPC sections (those references are read as references to the BNS equivalents: General Clauses Act s.8 and BNS s.358 construction clause). Example: POCSO and the Juvenile Justice Act contain IPC cross-references now read as BNS references.

case_laws.principle: A reduction of punishment by a later law operates for the benefit of the accused where the prosecution is still pending.

Art. 20(1) bars retrospective criminal laws and enhanced punishment; it does not bar retrospective ameliorative provisions.
Pending proceedings under CrPC continue under CrPC by virtue of BNSS s.531.
