ipc_bns_sections.title: Punishments in Depth: Death, Life Imprisonment, Remission, Fine, Forfeiture and Community Service
key_points: BNS s.4 lists six punishments: (a) death; (b) imprisonment for life; (c) imprisonment, which is either rigorous (with hard labour) or simple; (d) forfeiture of property; (e) fine; (f) community service (new).

Community service (BNS s.23 explanation, s.4(f) read with the Explanation): work which the court may direct a convict to perform for the benefit of the community, for which he shall not be entitled to any remuneration. It is intended as a non-custodial reformative alternative for petty and first-time offences. It is provided only in six provisions (see 4.1). The mode and manner of performance is left to the court; the details are to be framed through BNSS and rules [VERIFY].

Commutation (s.5): the appropriate Government may, without the consent of the offender, commute a death sentence to imprisonment for life, and imprisonment for life to imprisonment for a term not less than seven years; BNS removes the IPC 54 and 55 'any other punishment' language. Remission, suspension and commutation are also under BNSS ss.473-477 (CrPC 432-435) and Arts. 72 and 161 of the Constitution (Presidential and Governor's powers).

Imprisonment for life means imprisonment for the remainder of the convict's natural life, unless remitted by the appropriate Government under the statutory scheme (Gopal Vinayak Godse v State of Maharashtra, 1961; Mohd. Munna v Union of India, 2005). It is not equal to 20 years; the 20-year equivalence in s.6 is only for calculating fractions of terms. A convict sentenced to life cannot claim release after 14 years as of right: s.433A CrPC (BNSS 475) bars remission before 14 years' actual imprisonment in offences with a death punishment option.

Special category sentences: Swamy Shraddananda (2) v State of Karnataka (2008) allowed life imprisonment without remission for the entire life or a fixed term (e.g., 30 years) as an alternative to death; Union of India v V. Sriharan (2015): a five-judge Bench confirmed that the High Court and Supreme Court (not the trial court) may impose a modified punishment of life imprisonment for a specific period beyond 14 years or for the full natural life, without remission. The BNS adds explicit 'imprisonment for life for remainder of natural life' in the aggravated rape provisions.

Rigorous vs simple imprisonment (s.7): the court may direct that imprisonment shall be wholly rigorous, wholly simple, or partly each. Imprisonment in default of fine (s.8): where the fine is not paid, the court may direct imprisonment in default; the term shall not exceed one-fourth of the maximum term of imprisonment for the offence when the offence is punishable with both imprisonment and fine; the default imprisonment may be of any description for which the offender might have been sentenced for the offence.

Fine (s.8): where no sum is expressed, the amount of fine is unlimited but shall not be excessive. Where the offence is punishable with fine only, imprisonment in default may be of either description; where it is punishable with imprisonment as well, the default term cannot exceed one-fourth of the maximum term of imprisonment fixed for the offence. The IPC scale linking the amount of fine to the length of default imprisonment has been revised in the BNS; check the bare act for the present limits [VERIFY]. Death of the offender does not discharge his property from liability for the fine.

Limit of punishment for offences made up of several offences (s.9; IPC 71): where an offence is made up of parts, each of which is an offence, the offender shall not be punished for more than one of the offences unless expressly provided; the court should not award more than the maximum for the graver offence; this embodies the rule against double punishment for the same act.

Punishment of a person guilty of one of several offences (s.10; IPC 72): where it is doubtful of which offence the accused is guilty, he may be punished for the offence for which the lesser punishment is provided.

Solitary confinement (ss.11-12; IPC 73-74): the court may order that a convict sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for an offence for which solitary confinement is permitted shall be kept in solitary confinement for a portion of the term, not exceeding 3 months in the whole where the term is more than one year; not exceeding one month where the term does not exceed 6 months; not exceeding 14 days at a time with intervals; subject to the Supreme Court's decisions in Sunil Batra v Delhi Administration (1978) (solitary confinement on a convict under death sentence unconstitutional pre-execution) and Shatrughan Chauhan (2014).

Enhanced punishment after previous conviction (s.13; IPC 75): a person previously convicted of an offence under Chapter XII or XVII of the IPC (coins and stamps; property) punishable with imprisonment of three years or more is liable on a subsequent conviction to imprisonment for life or up to ten years. The BNS also builds repeat-offender enhancements into specific offences (for example theft, snatching, stalking and voyeurism) [VERIFY the exact text of s.13].

Forfeiture of property and attachment: s.4(d) retains forfeiture as a punishment; however, in practice it is used in organised crime (s.111) and terror provisions, and BNSS ss.107 (attachment, forfeiture or restoration of property: proceeds of crime) provides the procedure. BNSS s.107 is a major new power allowing the court, on the police officer's application with the Superintendent of Police's approval, to attach proceeds of crime [VERIFY].

Probation and alternatives: Probation of Offenders Act, 1958 (ss.3, 4, 6) allows release on admonition or on probation for good conduct for first offenders; s.360 CrPC (BNSS s.401) similar; rule: probation is not available where the offence is punishable with death or life; for persons below 21 and women the court shall record reasons for refusing probation (s.6 of the 1958 Act; s.360(3)). Compounding of offences under BNSS s.359 (CrPC 320) lists compoundable offences; BNSS expanded the list modestly [VERIFY].

Victim compensation and fine: BNSS s.395 (CrPC 357) allows the court to order that the fine be applied for compensation; s.396 (CrPC 357A) victim compensation scheme; the Supreme Court in Ankush Shivaji Gaikwad v State of Maharashtra (2013) held that courts should consider compensation in every case; and Laxmi (2014) for acid victims.

Death penalty procedure: BNSS 393(3) (CrPC 354(3)): when the conviction is for an offence punishable with death or alternatively with life imprisonment, the judgment shall state special reasons for the sentence of death. Confirmation by High Court: BNSS ss.407-409 (CrPC 366-368). Hanging by neck vs other methods: Deena v Union of India (1983) upheld hanging as a method; Attorney General v Lachma Devi (1986) public hanging unconstitutional. Execution of the pregnant woman or insane person: not permissible by law; Shatrughan Chauhan (2014) held that supervening insanity and inordinate delay in disposal of mercy petition are grounds for commutation.

Capital punishment under BNS: murder (103(1)), murder by a life convict (104), mob lynching (103(2)), rape causing death or persistent vegetative state (66), rape of a girl under 12 (65(2)), gang rape of a girl under 18 (70(2)), repeat rape offenders (71), organised crime resulting in death (111(2)(a)), terrorist act resulting in death (113(2)(a)), kidnapping for ransom (140(2)), dacoity with murder (310(3)), abetment of suicide of a child (107), waging war (147), abetment of mutiny, giving false evidence leading to execution of an innocent person (s.230) etc. Death is the exclusive punishment in only a few provisions and BNS has not retained a mandatory death sentence except where the Supreme Court has not struck it down (e.g., the IPC 303 position was struck down in Mithu; BNS 104 is framed in the alternative) [VERIFY].

Juveniles: capital punishment and life imprisonment without release cannot be imposed on a child in conflict with law (Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, s.21); the maximum institutional period is three years for heinous offences tried as an adult in a children's court; see Shilpa Mittal v State of NCT of Delhi (2020): an offence for which maximum is 7 years but no minimum is a 'serious' offence, not 'heinous'.

ipc_bns_sections.title: Criminal Liability Doctrines: Mens Rea, Strict Liability, Vicarious and Corporate Liability, Omissions, Causation
key_points: Mens rea in Indian law is reflected in the words 'intentionally', 'knowingly', 'voluntarily', 'dishonestly', 'fraudulently', 'rashly', 'negligently', 'with intent to', 'having reason to believe' used in the definitions rather than as a general doctrine. The Code defines the relevant mental states in BNS s.2.

Intention vs knowledge: intention is the purpose or desire to produce a result; knowledge is awareness of the likely consequence without desire. Murder (s.101) clauses mix the two. Motive vs intention: motive is the reason; it is generally irrelevant to criminal liability but relevant to proof and sentencing. Intention is inferred from the nature of the act, the weapon, the part of the body, and the surrounding circumstances (Anda v State of Rajasthan, 1966).

Rashness vs negligence: rashness is conscious taking of risk with the knowledge that the act may cause harm but hoping it will not; negligence is failure to exercise the care a reasonable man would exercise (Nidamarti Nagabhushanam v State of Karnataka, 2008). Gross negligence is required for criminal liability of professionals (Jacob Mathew) and in 304A (Kurban Hussein Mohammedali Rangwalla v State of Maharashtra, 1965: the act must be the proximate cause).

Strict liability: presumption of mens rea in statutory offences is rebuttable by the words of the statute and the object (Sherras v De Rutzen, 1895; State of Maharashtra v M.H. George, 1965; Gammon (Hong Kong) v Attorney-General (1985)); typically in public welfare, food adulteration, customs and revenue statutes. The Indian Penal Code provisions themselves require mens rea, subject to a few exceptions (e.g., sale of adulterated food), while mens rea is generally irrelevant under the 'public welfare' statutes.

Vicarious liability: ordinarily unknown in IPC/BNS offences; it arises only where the statute so provides (e.g., Food Safety and Standards Act, Negotiable Instruments Act s.141, Drugs and Cosmetics Act, Essential Commodities Act). Sham Sunder v State of Haryana (1989): partners cannot be vicariously liable for IPC offences without a specific allegation; Maksud Saiyed v State of Gujarat (2008): directors are not vicariously liable for IPC offences of the company unless the Code provides or specific overt acts are alleged; Sunil Bharti Mittal v CBI (2015): vicarious criminal liability of directors needs the company to be arraigned and the director to be the 'alter ego'.

Corporate criminal liability: a company is a 'person' under BNS s.2 (the 'person' definition includes any company or association or body of persons, whether incorporated or not). Standard Chartered Bank v Directorate of Enforcement (2005): a company can be prosecuted even for offences requiring mandatory imprisonment; the court may impose the fine alone; Iridium India Telecom v Motorola (2011): the company is liable for offences involving mens rea through the 'directing mind and will' (identification doctrine); Aneeta Hada v Godfather Travels (2012): director cannot be prosecuted under NI Act s.141 without arraigning the company.

Omissions: an 'act' includes a series of acts and 'illegal omission' (BNS s.2). Liability for omission arises where there is a legal duty to act (statute, contract, special relationship, assumption of duty, creating a danger): the parent who starves a child, the doctor under duty to treat, the gatekeeper who fails to alert. Illustrations: death by starvation of a ward by the guardian is murder or culpable homicide; omission to give food is covered by 'illegal omission'.

Causation: the act must be the 'proximate' or 'direct' cause of the result; novus actus interveniens breaks the chain if the intervening act is independent and unforeseeable. Concurrent causes (causing death even if the victim was already weak: 'thin skull' rule; BNS s.100 Explanation 1: the death of a person suffering from a disease or bodily infirmity hastened by the act is homicide). Explanation 2: causing bodily injury which, with proper treatment, could have been prevented: the injurer is liable. Explanation 3: causing the death of a child in the mother's womb is not homicide, but the death of a living child, any part of which has been brought forth, may be culpable homicide even if the child is not completely born.

Joint-property and group issues: the Code treats 'every act done by several persons' in BNS s.3(6); co-operation by doing one of several acts (s.3(7)); acts caused partly by an act and partly by omission (s.3(8)); cooperation by several persons in a criminal act (s.3(9)). Each of these explanations is expressly in the 'General Explanations' chapter.

'Voluntarily' (s.2): causing an effect by means whereby the person intended to cause it or by means which, at the time of employing them, he knew or had reason to believe to be likely to cause it. 'Good faith' (s.2): nothing is said to be done or believed in good faith which is done or believed without due care and attention.

'Dishonestly' (s.2) and 'fraudulently' (s.2): dishonesty needs wrongful gain or loss; fraud requires intention to defraud, which involves deceit and injury or risk of injury even if no wrongful gain (Dr Vimla v Delhi Administration; S. Dutt v State of UP, 1966).

'Public servant' (s.2): defined by a long list that includes every commissioned officer in the military, naval or air forces, every judge, every officer of a court, every arbitrator, every person authorised to perform election duties, every officer of the Government, and every officer in the service or pay of a local authority or of a corporation established by or under a Central, Provincial or State Act or a Government company; the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 has its own definition in s.2(c). Whether the staff of a body are public servants depends on whether they fall within the statutory list [VERIFY the clause number in BNS s.2].

ipc_bns_sections.title: Death Penalty and Sentencing Jurisprudence: Rarest of Rare, Mitigation, Mercy Petitions
key_points: Jagmohan Singh v State of UP (1973): the Supreme Court upheld the death penalty under Arts. 14, 19 and 21, saying sentencing discretion is guided by judicial discretion after the trial. Rajendra Prasad v State of UP (1979): death only in extraordinary cases where the community cannot be protected; individual-centric. Bachan Singh v State of Punjab (1980): Constitution Bench (4:1) upheld the death penalty, but only in the 'rarest of rare' cases when the alternative of life imprisonment is unquestionably foreclosed; the court must weigh aggravating and mitigating circumstances (the 'balance sheet' approach), with the mitigating being generously considered. Dissent: Justice P.N. Bhagwati (1982 reported) found the death penalty unconstitutional.

Machhi Singh v State of Punjab (1983): five categories - manner of commission (extreme brutality), motive (depravity), anti-social or socially abhorrent nature (e.g., bride burning or dowry death), magnitude (multiple murders), personality of the victim (child, helpless woman, public figure). Both tests: the 'crime test' and 'criminal test' are to be satisfied (Sangeet v State of Haryana, 2013 criticised the categorisation approach).

Santosh Kumar Bariyar (2009): the court must consider the circumstances of the criminal as well as the crime; the 'rarest of rare' test is not subjective. Sangeet v State of Haryana (2013): the aggravating and mitigating circumstances cannot be balanced in the abstract; the court must look at the offender. Manoj v State of Madhya Pradesh (2022): three-judge Bench laid down that the trial court must call for psychiatric and psychological evaluation reports, prison conduct reports and a social investigation report before sentencing in capital cases; sentencing is a separate, individualised exercise. Irfan v State of MP (2023) followed Manoj on mitigation; a Constitution Bench reference on the procedure for death-sentencing (In Re: Framing Guidelines Regarding Potential Mitigating Circumstances) has been pending [VERIFY current status].

Mithu v State of Punjab (1983): mandatory death penalty under IPC s.303 is unconstitutional (Arts. 14 and 21). Subsequent cases struck down mandatory death penalty in other statutes (e.g., Section 27(3) Arms Act in State of Punjab v Dalbir Singh, 2012; NDPS s.31A in Indian Harm Reduction Network v UoI, 2011 (Bombay HC) read down).

Mercy petition and delay: Triveniben v State of Gujarat (1989): delay may be a ground to commute but only where it is inordinate and unexplained; Shatrughan Chauhan v UoI (2014): inordinate delay in disposal of mercy petitions, solitary confinement, mental illness - grounds for commutation; Vatheeswaran v State of TN (1983) delay of two years sufficient (overruled in Sher Singh and in Triveniben). The President and Governor exercise the mercy power on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers (Maru Ram v UoI, 1981; Kehar Singh v UoI, 1989: the President can examine the evidence afresh; the courts cannot review on merits, only on limited grounds: Epuru Sudhakar v State of AP, 2006).

Review and curative petitions: Mohd. Arif @ Ashfaq v Registrar, Supreme Court (2014): review petitions in death cases are to be heard in open court by a Bench of at least three judges; execution is stayed pending. Yakub Memon (2015), Nirbhaya (2020) - curative petitions and the use of 'serial' mercy petitions.

Aggravating circumstances commonly accepted: murder of a child, rape-murder, premeditated multiple murders, murder for gain, torture and mutilation, murder of a public servant, terrorism; mitigating: young age (though not decisive), no prior record, probability of reformation, good conduct in jail, mental or emotional disturbance, circumstantial evidence only (the courts have repeatedly said that a death sentence on circumstantial evidence requires extra caution, but it is not a bar: Bishnu Prasad Sinha v State of Assam, 2007).

Executions and notable post-2000 cases: Dhananjoy Chatterjee (2004, executed for rape-murder), Ajmal Kasab (2012 SC; executed Nov 2012), Afzal Guru (2013), Yakub Memon (2015), the four Nirbhaya convicts (March 2020). Recent trend: the Supreme Court has commuted several death sentences into fixed-term life imprisonment, emphasising reformation and mitigation [VERIFY recent cases].

Constitutional questions pending: whether the method of hanging violates dignity (Rishi Malhotra's PIL, 2023 - SC asked the Union to examine alternatives such as lethal injection) [VERIFY status]. Statistics: Project 39A's annual report on death penalty in India (national law university) is the standard source; trial courts impose large numbers, the Supreme Court confirms very few.

AIBE angle: questions typically ask: which case laid down the rarest of rare doctrine; which struck down mandatory death sentence; who may commute; what is the effect of delay; the mode of execution; whether juvenile can be sentenced to death (no).

ipc_bns_sections.title: Murder, Culpable Homicide and Allied Offences: Advanced Doctrines and Case Analysis
key_points: Chart for answering problems: (1) Was there an act causing death? (2) Was there intention or knowledge as in s.100? If no, consider s.106 (negligence) or accident. (3) If yes, does any of the four clauses of s.101 apply? If no, culpable homicide not amounting to murder. (4) If yes, does any Exception 1-5 apply? If yes, culpable homicide; Part I or Part II punishment depends on intention/knowledge.

Section 100 Explanations: (1) causing the death of a person suffering from a disorder, disease or bodily infirmity, and thereby accelerating death, is culpable homicide; (2) where death is caused by bodily injury, the person causing the injury is deemed to have caused the death although proper remedies or skilful treatment might have prevented death; (3) causing the death of a child in the mother's womb is not homicide, but causing the death of a living child, any part of which has been brought forth, may amount to homicide even though the child has not breathed or been completely born.

Clause (b) of s.101 (IPC 300 'secondly'): intention to cause bodily injury which the offender knows is likely to cause the death of the particular person: requires subjective knowledge about the victim's condition (e.g., blow on the head of a known weak person). Clause (c) (thirdly): objective test of 'sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death': Virsa Singh; Rajwant Singh v State of Kerala (1966): the injury need not be intended to cause death; intended injury sufficient is enough. Clause (d) (fourthly): act imminently dangerous (firing in a crowd, shooting at random); no intention to harm particular person; knowledge that it must in all probability cause death

Exception 1 (grave and sudden provocation): conditions - (i) the provocation must be grave and sudden; (ii) it must deprive the offender of self-control; (iii) death must be of the person who gave the provocation or by accident or mistake of another; the provocation must not be sought or voluntarily provoked; not given by anything done in obedience to law or by a public servant in the lawful exercise of powers or in the lawful exercise of private defence. Cases: Nanavati; Ghapoo Yadav v State of MP (2003); Budhi Singh v State of HP (2012): words and gestures may amount to provocation depending on the person's standing; the Court considers the test of a reasonable man of the same class; Mancini v DPP is the English parallel. Confession of marital infidelity: courts have been reluctant when there is a time lapse; a plea of provocation is lost where there is cooling time.

Exception 2 (exceeding the right of private defence): act done in good faith in exercise of private defence, exceeds the power given by law, causes death without premeditation and without any intention of doing more harm than necessary. The Exception sits between acquittal (full private defence) and murder: Partap v State of UP (1976). Courts have cautioned that the accused who initiates the attack cannot claim this exception.

Exception 3 (public servant or aiding public servant): the act is done in the advancement of public justice, in good faith, exceeding the powers given by law, without ill-will; e.g., a policeman exceeding the law in making an arrest. Exception 4 (sudden fight): conditions - sudden fight, without premeditation, in the heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel, and the offender has not taken undue advantage or acted in a cruel or unusual manner: Surinder Kumar v Union Territory, Chandigarh (1989); Gurmukh Singh v State of Haryana (2009); the court looks at who started the fight, the weapon, the number of blows. Exception 5 (consent): the person killed is above 18 and suffers death or takes the risk with his own consent (e.g., a duel; euthanasia attempts historically): consent must be free and informed; passive euthanasia under Aruna Shanbaug (2011) and Common Cause v UoI (2018) is permitted for terminally ill patients, with advance directives guided by the Court's procedure, modified in January 2023 for simplification.

Culpable homicide not amounting to murder: Part I of s.105 (IPC 304 first part): act done with the intention of causing death or such bodily injury as is likely to cause death (but covered by an exception) - life or up to 10 years and fine; Part II: act done with knowledge that it is likely to cause death but without intention - up to 10 years or fine or both. Sentence is determined by the nature of the weapon, circumstances, and whether the accused took advantage.

Thin dividing lines in cases: Reg v Govinda (1876) - husband kicked wife, causing a bleeding; no intention to cause death; held culpable homicide. Pulicherla Nagaraju v State of AP (2006): factors - nature of the weapon, parts of the body, force used, the circumstances, premeditation, the number of blows. Rampal Singh v State of UP (2012): 'intention to cause death' vs 'knowledge'; the accused who aimed a gun at vital parts is guilty of murder.

Dowry death vs murder: dowry death is a separate offence requiring proof of cruelty or harassment for dowry soon before death within 7 years of marriage, with the burden of proof shifting to the accused through the statutory presumption (BSA s.118); the same facts can attract s.80 (dowry death), s.85 (cruelty), s.108 (abetment of suicide) and s.103 (murder) in the alternative. The Supreme Court has held that, if the death is homicidal, it is not 'dowry death' as 'otherwise than under normal circumstances' covers both; the court may convict under s.304B even if murder is not proved (Kans Raj; Hira Lal).

Negligence offences: death by rash or negligent act (s.106(1)); medical negligence: Jacob Mathew prescribes the Bolam test with a higher threshold for criminal negligence, that the practitioner is liable only if no reasonable practitioner would have done the same; a private complaint against a doctor requires a credible opinion of another competent doctor (BNSS procedure for doctors; BNS s.106(1) proviso punishes up to 2 years for registered medical practitioners). Rash and negligent driving: s.281; s.106(1); hit and run: s.106(2) (see 4.5). Drunk driving causing death: culpable homicide where knowledge is shown (Alister Anthony Pareira).

Attempt to murder vs hurt: 'intention or knowledge' and 'under such circumstances that if death had been caused he would be guilty of murder': hurt need not be caused (Sarju Prasad v State of Bihar, 1965: firing at a person with intent to kill is attempt even if no injury results). The second part of s.109 (hurt caused: life or up to 10 years) applies where hurt is caused to the person attacked.

ipc_bns_sections.title: Marriage, Dowry and Domestic Cruelty: BNS ss.80-86 with Dowry Prohibition Act and Domestic Violence Act
key_points: Offences relating to marriage in BNS: cohabitation caused by a man deceitfully inducing a belief of lawful marriage (s.81; IPC 493): up to 10 years and fine; bigamy (s.82(1); IPC 494): up to 7 years and fine; bigamy with concealment of the former marriage (s.82(2); IPC 495): up to 10 years and fine; marriage ceremony fraudulently gone through without lawful marriage (s.83; IPC 496): up to 7 years and fine; enticing, taking away or detaining a married woman with criminal intent (s.84; IPC 498): up to 2 years or fine or both. Adultery (IPC 497) has been omitted after Joseph Shine (2018), so a husband has no criminal remedy against his wife's paramour, and vice versa.

Bigamy ingredients: (i) accused has a living spouse; (ii) he marries again; (iii) the second marriage is void by reason of the spouse's being alive; (iv) the first marriage is valid and subsisting. Both marriages must be proved with valid ceremonies: Bhaurao Shankar Lokhande v State of Maharashtra (1965): 'solemnised' means celebrated with proper ceremonies and in due form; mere admission is insufficient. Priya Bala Ghosh v Suresh Chandra Ghosh (1971) and Kanwal Ram v Himachal Pradesh Administration (1966): essential ceremonies (saptapadi) must be proved. Sarla Mudgal v UoI (1995) and Lily Thomas v UoI (2000): conversion to Islam to marry again does not dissolve the first marriage; the second marriage is void and bigamy applies. Exception: marriage declared void by a court of competent jurisdiction; spouse continually absent for seven years and not heard of as alive.

Section 85 (IPC 498A): husband or relative of husband subjecting a woman to cruelty: up to 3 years and fine. Section 86 defines cruelty: (a) wilful conduct likely to drive the woman to commit suicide or to cause grave injury or danger to life, limb or health, mental or physical; (b) harassment of the woman where such harassment is with a view to coercing her or any person related to her to meet any unlawful demand for property or valuable security, or on account of failure by her or her relatives to meet such demand. Offence is cognizable, non-bailable and non-compoundable under the CrPC schedule; the Supreme Court in Gian Singh v State of Punjab (2012) and B.S. Joshi v State of Haryana (2003) has permitted the High Court to quash matrimonial cases under its inherent powers where the parties settle.

'Relative of the husband' under 498A: includes blood relatives and persons related by marriage; U. Suvetha v State (2009): a woman living with the husband as a concubine is not a 'relative'; Vijeta Gajra v State (NCT of Delhi) (2010): a woman living in a live-in relationship is not a 'relative' for 498A (this was resolved differently in subsequent cases; the BNS Explanation does not extend it) [VERIFY].

Misuse of 498A and safeguards: Sushil Kumar Sharma v Union of India (2005) upheld constitutionality but called misuse 'legal terrorism'; Arnesh Kumar v State of Bihar (2014): arrests only after satisfaction that the grounds in s.41 CrPC (BNSS 35) exist; the magistrate must not authorise detention mechanically; notice of appearance in cases where punishment is up to 7 years; Rajesh Sharma v State of UP (2017) directed Family Welfare Committees, which was set aside in Social Action Forum for Manav Adhikar v UoI (2018); Preeti Gupta v State of Jharkhand (2010): the courts should be cautious about omnibus allegations against distant relatives; Kahkashan Kausar v State of Bihar (2022): the vague, general allegations against in-laws are insufficient; Achin Gupta v State of Haryana (2024): the Supreme Court observed that cases cannot be continued on bald allegations [VERIFY]; Mahmood Ali v State of UP (2023): reiterated that FIR quashing is justified if the criminal proceeding is used for personal vendetta; Dara Lakshmi Narayana v State of Telangana (2024): reiterated protection against general and omnibus allegations in dowry and cruelty complaints [VERIFY]. Parliament has not carried forward any gender-neutral amendment; the Parliamentary Standing Committee in 2023 recommended a gender-neutral provision in the context of rape and unnatural offences but the Sanhita retained the woman-victim framework for ss.63-99 [VERIFY].

Dowry death (s.80; IPC 304B): ingredients: (i) death of a woman caused by burns or bodily injury or otherwise than under normal circumstances; (ii) within seven years of her marriage; (iii) soon before her death she was subjected to cruelty or harassment by her husband or any relative of her husband; (iv) the cruelty or harassment was for, or in connection with, any demand for dowry. Explanation: 'dowry' has the same meaning as in Section 2 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961. Punishment: imprisonment not less than 7 years, which may extend to imprisonment for life. Presumption: where it is shown that soon before her death the woman was subjected to cruelty or harassment for dowry, the court shall presume that such person caused the dowry death (BSA s.118; Evidence Act s.113B). Burden shifts to the accused; the presumption is rebuttable.

Interplay: Section 304B and Section 302 are not mutually exclusive; if homicidal death with dowry harassment is proved, the court can convict for murder and dowry death in the alternative but cannot punish twice for the same act (Satbir Singh; Kaliyaperumal v State of TN, 2003). Suicide within seven years with dowry harassment may amount to both 304B and abetment of suicide (s.108) with presumption under BSA s.117 (Evidence Act 113A: presumption as to abetment of suicide by a married woman within seven years of marriage, if she was subjected to cruelty). The words 'soon before' do not fix a time limit: Kans Raj; Rajinder Singh v State of Punjab (2015): there must be a proximate and live link between the effect of cruelty and the death.

Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961: giving, taking or abetting the giving or taking of dowry (s.3): imprisonment not less than 5 years and fine not less than Rs 15,000 or the value of the dowry, whichever is more; demanding dowry (s.4): imprisonment not less than 6 months extendable to 2 years and fine up to Rs 10,000; advertisement offering share in property as consideration for marriage (s.4A); burden of proof on the person who takes or abets the taking of dowry (s.8A); dowry given for the benefit of the wife must be transferred to her within three months (s.6); offences under the Act are cognizable, non-bailable and non-compoundable (s.8). Gifts given at the time of marriage without demand and entered in a list are excluded from dowry (s.3(2)). Dowry Prohibition Officers are appointed by State Governments (s.8B). Pratibha Rani v Suraj Kumar (1985): stridhan remains the wife's absolute property; a husband or in-laws who dishonestly misappropriate it commit CBT (s.316, previously IPC 406). Rashmi Kumar v Mahesh Kumar Bhada (1997) confirmed entrustment of stridhan to the husband.

Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005: civil law remedies - protection orders, residence orders (right to shared household: S.R. Batra v Taruna Batra (2007); Satish Chander Ahuja v Sneha Ahuja (2020): shared household includes a household in which the woman lived with her husband, not limited to property owned by him), monetary relief, custody and compensation. Breach of a protection order is a criminal offence (s.31: imprisonment up to 1 year and fine up to Rs 20,000). 'Domestic relationship' includes live-in relationships ('relationship in the nature of marriage': D. Velusamy v D. Patchaiammal, 2010; Indra Sarma v V.K.V. Sarma, 2013: the criteria of duration, shared household, pooling of resources etc.). 'Respondent' includes male adult only (the proviso allows woman respondent in the case of a relative); Hiral P. Harsora v Kusum Narottamdas Harsora (2016) struck down the words 'adult male' to allow complaints against women relatives. Maintenance: Section 125 CrPC (BNSS s.144) is available to wives, children and parents; Rajnesh v Neha (2020) lays down guidelines on maintenance (disclosure of assets and liabilities affidavit); Mohd. Ahmed Khan v Shah Bano Begum (1985) and Danial Latifi v UoI (2001) for Muslim women's maintenance; Shabana Bano v Imran Khan (2009); Mohd. Abdul Samad v State of Telangana (2024): a divorced Muslim woman can claim maintenance under s.125 CrPC and not only under the 1986 Act [VERIFY].

Marital rape: Exception 2 to s.63: sexual intercourse by a man with his own wife, the wife not being under 18, is not rape. Independent Thought v UoI (2017) read down the earlier 15-year limit to 18. The Delhi High Court delivered a split verdict in RIT Foundation v UoI (May 2022); the Karnataka High Court (Hrishikesh Sahoo v State of Karnataka, 2022) allowed a rape charge to be framed against a husband; the Supreme Court has the challenge pending [VERIFY current status]. Separately, s.67 (IPC 376B) penalises sexual intercourse with a wife living separately under a decree of separation or otherwise, without her consent: 2 to 7 years and fine.

Section 84 (IPC 498): enticing or taking away or detaining with criminal intent a married woman, not the husband: the offence is against the husband's right and not the wife; since Joseph Shine (2018) the gender-biased scheme is criticised, though the provision remains; the offence requires the woman to be 'taken away' or 'enticed' with the intent that she may have illicit intercourse with any person.

Related procedural points: BNSS provides for medical examination of rape victims, recording of statements by a woman magistrate or officer, and video recording of statements (BNSS s.173(1) read with s.176: audio-video recording of search and statement of rape victims); trials in camera (BNSS s.366(2)); time limit of two months for completing investigation in rape cases (BNSS s.193(2)) and trial within two months of framing charges (CrPC 309: BNSS 346); zero FIR (BNSS s.173(1)); e-FIR (BNSS s.173(1)(ii)) [VERIFY references].

ipc_bns_sections.title: Sexual Offences: Evidence, Consent, Child Victims (POCSO), Victim Protection and Recent Law
key_points: Rape under BNS s.63: sexual intercourse with a woman in the seven circumstances; penetration to any extent is sufficient; Explanation: penetration includes insertion of any object or a part of the body (not being the penis) into the vagina, urethra or anus; manipulation of body parts; application of mouth. Penetration suffices; emission or rupture of the hymen is not necessary (State of UP v Babul Nath, 1994).

Consent: Explanation 2 to s.63: consent means an unequivocal voluntary agreement when the woman by words, gestures or any form of verbal or non-verbal communication communicates willingness to participate in the specific sexual act; a woman who does not physically resist shall not by the reason only of that fact be regarded as consenting. Cases: Uday v State of Karnataka (2003): consent obtained on a promise of marriage is 'under a misconception of fact' only if the promise was false from the start and the woman's decision was caused by it; Deepak Gulati v State of Haryana (2013): distinction between rape and consensual sex; the court must examine whether the accused had the intention to marry at the time; Pramod Suryabhan Pawar (2019); Naim Ahamed v State (NCT of Delhi) (2023): a long-standing consensual relationship cannot be converted into rape on a failed marriage promise; the court cautioned about the abuse of the rape law where parties were in a consensual relationship and the allegation arises after the breakdown [VERIFY]. BNS s.69 now separately criminalises a promise of marriage made with no intention to fulfil it.

Prosecutrix testimony: the conviction can be based on the sole testimony of the prosecutrix if it inspires confidence (State of Punjab v Gurmit Singh (1996); State of UP v Chhoteylal (2011)); corroboration is not a rule of law but a rule of prudence; the court should not insist on medical evidence if the testimony is reliable; delay in lodging FIR is not fatal where explained (State of Himachal Pradesh v Shree Kant Shekari, 2004); a prior sexual history is irrelevant (BSA s.151(4); Evidence Act s.146 proviso) - questioning on the victim's character or previous sexual experience to establish consent is prohibited.

'Two-finger test' is unconstitutional and violates the right to privacy and dignity: Lillu @ Rajesh v State of Haryana (2013); State of Jharkhand v Shailendra Kumar Rai (2022) directed that those conducting it be treated as guilty of misconduct. Medical examination of the victim under BNSS 184 (CrPC 164A) is to be done by a registered medical practitioner with consent, within 24 hours of the receipt of information.

Mathura rape case (Tukaram v State of Maharashtra, 1979) triggered the Criminal Law (Second Amendment) Act, 1983: introduction of s.376(2) aggravated rape (custodial rape), s.114A of the Evidence Act (presumption as to absence of consent), in camera trials and prohibition on disclosing victim identity; the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act 2013 (post-Nirbhaya) widened the definition, added acid attack, stalking, voyeurism, sexual harassment; the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act 2018 (Kathua and Unnao) added death penalty for rape of girls under 12 and minimum punishment of 20 years for girls below 16.

Gang rape (s.70): where a woman is raped by one or more persons constituting a group or acting in furtherance of a common intention, each of those persons is deemed to have committed gang rape; no separate proof of individual penetration is needed; punishment 20 years to life (natural life) and a fine just and reasonable to meet medical expenses and rehabilitation of the victim, which shall be paid to the victim; gang rape of a woman under 18: life (natural life) or death. Mukesh (Nirbhaya, 2017): gang-rape and murder.

Persons in authority and custody (s.64(2); s.68): rape by a police officer within the limits of the police station, public servant, member of armed forces deployed in an area, jail or remand home staff, management or staff of a hospital, a relative, guardian or teacher, a person in a position of trust or authority; committing rape during communal or sectarian violence; rape on a woman knowing her to be pregnant; rape of a woman incapable of giving consent; repeated rape of the same woman; causing grievous bodily harm, maiming, disfiguring or endangering life; rape of a mentally or physically disabled woman. Minimum 10 years, may extend to life for the remainder of natural life. Custodial rape: State of Maharashtra v Chandraprakash Kewalchand Jain (1990).

Victim identity and compensation: s.72 (IPC 228A): disclosure of the name or any matter which may identify the victim is punishable with up to 2 years and fine; the exception is where disclosure is authorised by the victim in writing, by the next of kin if she is dead or a minor, or on the authority of the police officer investigating; the printing of court proceedings relating to such offences without the permission of the court is punishable under s.73. Nipun Saxena v Union of India (2018) extended the bar to all documents and held that even in judgments of the High Court the victim's name should not be disclosed; the next of kin cannot authorise disclosure except to a recognised welfare institution. Compensation: Nirbhaya Fund; Section 357A CrPC (BNSS 396) State schemes; the Supreme Court in Delhi Domestic Working Women's Forum v UoI (1995) directed the establishment of a Criminal Injuries Compensation Board.

Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 (POCSO): applies to a 'child', any person below 18 years (s.2(d)); it is gender neutral; it covers penetrative sexual assault (s.3), punishable under s.4 with imprisonment not less than 10 years, extendable to life and fine (for a child below 16: not less than 20 years, extendable to life, meaning the remainder of natural life); aggravated penetrative sexual assault (s.5) punishable under s.6 with not less than 20 years to life or death (after the 2019 amendment); sexual assault (s.7), punishable under s.8 with 3 to 5 years; aggravated sexual assault (s.9) punishable under s.10 with 5 to 7 years; sexual harassment (s.11), punishable under s.12 with up to 3 years; use of child for pornographic purposes (s.13), punishable under s.14 with not less than 5 years (7 years on subsequent conviction); storage of pornographic material involving a child (s.15) with fines up to Rs 5,000 for first conviction, and 3 years for sharing, etc.

POCSO procedure and presumptions: mandatory reporting of knowledge or apprehension of an offence (s.19); failure to report is punishable with up to 6 months (s.21); the Special Court (s.28); child-friendly procedures: statement of the child at the residence or a place of choice, by a woman sub-inspector, in plain clothes, with the support of a parent or person of the child's trust (s.24); no child shall be detained in the police station at night (s.24(4)); the identity of the child is to be protected (s.23); presumption as to the commission of the offence (s.29) and a presumption of culpable mental state (s.30), subject to the standard of proof beyond a reasonable doubt for the accused's rebuttal by preponderance; speedy trial: the Special Court is to complete the trial within one year (s.35(2)). Special Court may order interim compensation (s.33(8)).

Key POCSO cases: Attorney General for India v Satish (2021): 'skin to skin contact' is not required for sexual assault under s.7; the touching of a child's body parts with sexual intent is sufficient; the Bombay High Court judgment (Pushpa Ganediwala) was set aside; Independent Thought (2017): the interplay between POCSO and the marital rape exception for a girl between 15 and 18; Just Rights for Children Alliance v S. Harish (2024): the Supreme Court held that storing, possessing or viewing child pornography is an offence under s.15 POCSO and s.67B of the IT Act even without transmission, and it directed that the term 'child sexual exploitative and abuse material (CSEAM)' replace 'child pornography' in law [VERIFY]; Sakshi v Union of India (2004): in-camera and screen-protected testimony for child victims; State of Rajasthan v Om Prakash (2002).

Romantic relationships between adolescents: the Supreme Court and High Courts have noted the 'Romeo-Juliet' problem (consensual acts between persons aged 16-18) and recommended judicial sensitivity (Madras High Court in Vijaylakshmi v State (2021) suggested reconsidering the age of consent; Law Commission 283rd Report (2023) recommended retaining 18 years but providing judicial discretion in sentencing for tacit approval cases of 16-18 years) [VERIFY]. In Nipun Saxena and Independent Thought, the Court insisted on harmonising the Code with POCSO.

Juvenile justice linkages: Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015: a 'child' is below 18; heinous offences (minimum sentence 7 years or more) by a child aged 16-18 may be tried as an adult after a preliminary assessment by the Juvenile Justice Board; serious offences (punishable with 3 to 7 years) and petty offences (up to 3 years); no death penalty or life imprisonment without possibility of release for children; Shilpa Mittal (2020); Mukesh v State: the juvenile in Nirbhaya was tried under the 2000 Act and given the maximum three years in a special home before the 2015 Act was enacted.

Missing from BNS: the Sanhita omits the unnatural offences provision (IPC 377), which survived Navtej Singh Johar (2018) only for non-consensual acts, acts with minors and bestiality. This leaves male and transgender victims of non-consensual penetrative acts without a specific provision under the Sanhita (apart from other provisions like s.74-type assault) except POCSO for children; the Parliamentary Standing Committee had recommended retention in a gender-neutral form; the Government did not accept it. Hot topic for exam: Navtej Singh Johar decriminalised consensual same-sex acts between adults. The Supreme Court in Supriyo @ Supriya Chakraborty v UoI (2023) declined to recognise a right to same-sex marriage but recognised that the State must not discriminate and set up a committee on rights of queer couples. The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 defines transgender persons and prescribes imprisonment of 6 months to 2 years for sexual abuse; BNS defines 'gender' to include a transgender person (s.2(10)).

ipc_bns_sections.title: Property Offences Advanced: Theft, CBT, Cheating, Forgery and Mischief in Practice
key_points: Illustrations that recur: (a) A cuts down a tree on Z's ground to dishonestly take it: theft when the tree is severed; (b) A finds a purse on the road and keeps it believing the owner can be found: not theft but misappropriation if dishonest intention arises later; (c) A shopkeeper takes money entrusted to him for payment of a bill and uses it for himself: CBT; (d) a servant takes his master's money from the drawer: theft by servant (s.306) not CBT unless entrusted with possession or dominion; (e) a man says he will give a job for a bribe and takes money, knowing he cannot: cheating; (f) a man obtains a loan with a false statement of property: cheating by inducement; (g) A threatens to publish Z's secret unless paid: extortion; (h) A takes Z's cell phone by snatching from a rider of a two-wheeler: snatching (s.304).

Theft: possession - the possession of servant, wife or clerk is that of the master, husband or employer (Explanation 3-5 to s.303); possession of the owner is theft even if the thief is the co-owner who takes the property out of the possession of the other (Explanation). A person who takes his own property from the possession of a bailee, pledgee or lien-holder commits theft. 'Dishonestly' requires wrongful gain or loss: taking property in a bona fide claim of right is not theft (Chandi Kumar Das Karmarkar v Abanidra Kumar Das, 1972). The taking must be 'without consent' - consent may be express or implied; consent obtained by fraud is no consent. Theft of electricity: the Electricity Act s.135 governs, not the IPC: a special law prevails (Avtar Singh v State of Punjab, 2002 on theft of electricity: Section 135 applies; IPC is excluded as the Electricity Act is a complete code).

Extortion v Robbery: In extortion, the victim is put in fear and delivers the property. In robbery by extortion, the offender is present at the time of the delivery, puts the victim in fear of instant death, hurt or restraint, and obtains the property. Illustration: A holds a knife at Z and demands money; Z delivers: robbery. If A says, 'I will have your son killed next month unless you pay', and Z pays: extortion, not robbery. Fear must be of injury to person, reputation or property; the victim's consent is obtained by fear (R.S. Nayak v A.R. Antulay (1986) discussed the contention of extortion in the public servant context).

Dacoity: the number is the gist; the offence is complete even if only the attempt exists, and the members who are present, aiding or attempting count (s.310). The gang need not be armed; the presence of five or more persons conjointly attempting is enough. A conviction for dacoity requires proof that at least five persons participated; the prosecution must prove that five or more persons took part; if fewer than five are proved to have participated, the offence is robbery and not dacoity [VERIFY authorities].

Criminal misappropriation vs CBT: Dishonest misappropriation requires only 'possession' (innocent at first); CBT requires 'entrustment'. Illustration: A finds a ring and later sells it: misappropriation (s.314). A is given Z's ring for safe-keeping and sells it: CBT (s.316). Entrustment includes a bailment, trust, agency and dominion, even over money. Key authority: Jaswantrai Manilal Akhaney v State of Bombay (1956) - a director/bank officer's dominion over funds; Sudhir Shantilal Mehta v CBI (2009): the distinction between CBT and cheating: in CBT the entrustment is lawful at the beginning, whereas in cheating the dishonest intention is present at the time of inducement; Delhi Race Club (1940) Ltd v State of UP (2024): the Supreme Court held that cheating and CBT are different offences and that the same facts cannot ordinarily constitute both, since in cheating the dishonest intention exists at the inception, whereas in CBT the property is entrusted willingly; the Court quashed the summoning order for both offences in a case about breach of a contract [VERIFY].

Cheating vs breach of contract: Dishonest intention must exist at the time of making the promise: Hridaya Ranjan Prasad Verma; Vesa Holdings v State of Kerala (2015); Sarabjit Kaur v State of Punjab (2023): the court quashed a cheating complaint where the dispute was purely a failure to perform and dishonest intention at the inception was not established; Vijay Kumar Ghai v State of West Bengal (2022); Indian Oil Corporation v NEPC India Ltd (2006): the Supreme Court deprecated the growing tendency to give a criminal colour to commercial disputes; Mohd. Ibrahim v State of Bihar (2009): sale of the property of another is not forgery; but it may be cheating. In real estate disputes, the Supreme Court has repeatedly intervened to quash complaints that convert civil disputes into criminal cases.

Cheating by personation (s.319), cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property or making, altering or destroying a valuable security (s.318(4)): includes an offender's inducing a bank to disburse a loan on forged documents. A lottery or chit fund fraud may also attract the Banning of Unregulated Deposit Schemes Act, 2019 (BUDS Act). Online cheating: cheating by personation using a computer resource is also an offence under IT Act s.66D (up to 3 years and fine up to Rs 1 lakh); BNS ss.318-319 apply along with the IT Act; the cyber-fraud provisions interplay with organised crime s.111 where cyber crimes are part of a syndicate's continuing unlawful activity.

Mischief: Intent or knowledge of causing wrongful loss or damage; the act must cause destruction or diminution of value or utility; wrongful loss or damage is not required to be of monetary kind. Mischief by killing or maiming an animal; mischief by injury to works of irrigation, public roads, bridges, navigable rivers; mischief by fire or explosive substance with intent to destroy a house (life or up to 10 years). The Prevention of Damage to Public Property Act, 1984 is the special law. In Re: Destruction of Public and Private Properties v State of AP (2009): guidelines on liability of organisers of riots for damage to public property (reversing the burden); Kodungallur Film Society v UoI (2018): directions on mob violence damaging property.

Criminal trespass: entry on property in the possession of another with intent to commit an offence, or to intimidate, insult or annoy; or unlawful remaining after lawful entry with such intent. House trespass: criminal trespass in a building used as a human dwelling, a place of worship or a place for the custody of property. Lurking house trespass: house trespass after taking precautions to conceal the entry; house-breaking: entering by specific methods (a passage made by the trespasser, opening a lock, etc.); by night means after sunset and before sunrise. Trespass is an offence against possession, not ownership: a true owner who forcibly enters a house possessed by a tenant is guilty of trespass if he has intent to annoy.

Forgery: 'making a false document' (s.335; IPC 464) includes dishonestly or fraudulently making, signing, sealing or executing a document or part of it with the intention of causing it to be believed that it was made by the authority of a person by whom the maker knows it was not made; altering a document without authority after it has been made; causing a person who is incapable of knowing the contents to sign or alter. Electronic signatures and digital records are covered; a 'document' (s.2(8)) includes electronic and digital records. Forgery of a valuable security or will (s.338: life or up to 10 years); forgery for the purpose of cheating (s.336(3): up to 7 years). Using a forged document as genuine (s.340): punishment as if the user had forged it. Possession of a forged document with the intent to use it as genuine, making or possessing counterfeit seals (ss.338-343).

Falsification of accounts (s.344; IPC 477A): clerk, officer or servant wilfully and with intent to defraud destroys, alters, mutilates or falsifies any book, electronic record, paper, writing, valuable security or account that belongs to or is in the possession of his employer: up to 7 years or fine or both. Interplay with Companies Act s.447 and Prevention of Corruption Act. Property mark offences (ss.345-349): using a false property mark with intent to deceive (up to 1 year), counterfeiting a property mark used by another, and the Trade Marks Act 1999 provisions (ss.103-107) now cover most commercial counterfeiting (which are more specific than the IPC).

Offences relating to coins, banknotes and stamps (ss.178-188; IPC 230-263A): counterfeiting Indian coin (life or up to 10 years), counterfeiting currency notes or bank notes (s.179-180: life or up to 10 years and fine); possession of forged notes (s.181); and the newly added possession of counterfeit stamps. Recent emphasis on 'fake Indian currency notes (FICN)' as a terror finance concern; the BNS treats the counterfeiting of currency as an offence against the economic security of India under s.113 terrorist act where it affects economic security (s.113(1)(a) includes damage to the monetary stability of India by means of counterfeit or smuggled currency).

ipc_bns_sections.title: Public Servants, Contempt of Lawful Authority, False Evidence and Public Justice (Chapters X-XIII in Practice)
key_points: Chapter structure in BNS: offences by or relating to public servants (ss.198-205: including public servant unlawfully engaging in trade s.202 and unlawfully buying or bidding for property s.203, personating a public servant s.204, wearing garb or carrying a token used by a public servant with fraudulent intent s.205); contempt of lawful authority of public servants (ss.206-226); false evidence and offences against public justice (ss.227-269) [VERIFY section ranges].

Absconding to avoid service of summons or other proceeding (s.206; IPC 172): up to 1 month simple imprisonment or fine up to Rs 5,000 or both (if the summons relates to attendance in person or by agent: up to 6 months or fine up to Rs 10,000) [VERIFY]. Non-attendance in obedience to an order from a public servant (s.209; IPC 174): up to 1 month or fine up to Rs 1,000 or both, or community service; if the order requires attendance in person or by agent in a court: up to 6 months or fine up to Rs 5,000. Omission to produce a document (s.210), omission to give notice or information (s.211), furnishing false information (s.212), refusing oath (s.213), refusing to answer questions (s.214), refusing to sign statements (s.215), false statement on oath to a public servant (s.216), false information to a public servant (s.217), resistance to the taking of property by lawful authority (s.218), obstructing sale of property offered by lawful authority (s.219), illegal purchase or bid (s.220), obstructing a public servant in discharge of public functions (s.221), omission to assist a public servant (s.222), disobedience to an order duly promulgated by a public servant (s.223), threat of injury to a public servant (s.224), threat of injury to induce a person to refrain from applying for protection to a public servant (s.225), attempt to commit suicide to compel or restrain exercise of lawful power (s.226) [VERIFY numbering].

Disobedience to order duly promulgated (s.223; IPC 188): the offence requires knowledge of the order and that the disobedience causes or tends to cause obstruction, annoyance or injury to persons lawfully employed, danger to human life, health or safety, or a riot or affray. Prosecution requires a complaint in writing by the public servant concerned (BNSS s.215(1)(a); CrPC 195(1)(a)). Used frequently for Section 144-type orders (BNSS s.163): Anuradha Bhasin v Union of India (2020): orders under s.144 must be proportionate, reasoned and subject to judicial review; indefinite internet shutdown violates Arts. 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g); Ramlila Maidan Incident, In Re (2012): the police power under s.144 must be exercised in good faith and the right to assemble is subject to reasonable restrictions.

False evidence: ingredients - (i) a person is legally bound by an oath or by an express provision of law to state the truth, or is bound by law to make a declaration upon any subject; (ii) he makes a statement; (iii) the statement is false; (iv) he knows or believes it to be false or does not believe it to be true. The statement may be oral or in writing, and may be made to a court, a public servant or any other authority. Perjury: false evidence in judicial proceedings: up to 7 years and fine (s.229(1)); in other cases up to 3 years and fine. Fabricating false evidence: causing any circumstance to exist or making any false entry in a book, record or electronic record or making any document or electronic record containing a false statement, intending that it may appear in evidence in a judicial proceeding, to lead to a wrong opinion: s.228; punishment s.230 (same scale). Giving or fabricating false evidence with intent to procure a conviction of a capital offence: life or rigorous imprisonment up to 10 years and fine (s.230(1)); if an innocent person is executed in consequence: death or the same (s.230(2)); intent to procure conviction for an offence punishable with life or 7 years: up to 7 years and fine.

Perjury procedure: A court can take cognizance of s.229 only on the written complaint of that court (BNSS s.215(1)(b)(i); CrPC 195(1)(b)(i)); the court must record a finding that it is expedient in the interest of justice to initiate the prosecution (BNSS s.379; CrPC 340), and the inquiry is preliminary: Pritish v State of Maharashtra (2002): the court must form a prima facie opinion; Iqbal Singh Marwah v Meenakshi Marwah (2005): s.195(1)(b)(ii) applies only to documents forged after they are produced in court; Sachida Nand Singh v State of Bihar (1998): the bar does not apply to forgery before the document is filed.

Using evidence known to be false as true (s.231), issuing or signing a false certificate (s.232), using a certificate known to be false (s.233-234), false statement in any declaration which is by law receivable as evidence (s.236), causing disappearance of evidence of offence, or giving false information to screen offender (s.238), intentional omission to give information of offence by a person legally bound to inform (s.239), giving false information respecting an offence committed (s.240), destruction of a document or electronic record to prevent its production as evidence (s.241), false personation for the purpose of an act or proceeding in a suit (s.242), fraudulent removal or concealment of property to prevent its seizure (s.243), fraudulent claim to property (s.244) [VERIFY].

Harbouring an offender (ss.249-250; IPC 212-216A): harbouring an offender is punishable, with an exception for a spouse harbouring the other spouse; punishment depends on the gravity of the offence for which the offender is harboured (up to 5 years where the offence is punishable with death; up to 3 years where punishable with life imprisonment or imprisonment up to 10 years; one-fourth of the longest term in other cases). Taking a gift to screen an offender from punishment is a separate offence (IPC 213) [VERIFY BNS section numbers].

Offences relating to elections (BNS ss.169-177; IPC 171A-171I) [VERIFY]: bribery (s.170; IPC 171B): giving or accepting a gratification to induce a person to exercise or refrain from exercising an electoral right: up to 1 year or fine or both; treating is bribery by food, drink or entertainment; undue influence (s.171; IPC 171C): voluntary interference with the free exercise of any electoral right: up to 1 year or fine or both; personation at elections (s.172; IPC 171D): up to 1 year; false statement in connection with election (s.174; IPC 171G): fine only; illegal payments in connection with an election (s.175; IPC 171H): fine up to Rs 500; failure to keep election accounts (s.176; IPC 171I): fine up to Rs 500. The Representation of the People Act, 1951 (ss.123, 125-136) contains corrupt practices and electoral offences, with electoral disqualification under ss.8-8A. The Supreme Court in Abhiram Singh v C.D. Commachen (2017) (seven-judge Bench) interpreted the corrupt practice of seeking votes in the name of religion, race, caste, community or language under s.123(3) RPA to include the religion of the candidate, the voter and the agent; in Union of India v Association for Democratic Reforms (2002) and PUCL v UoI (2003), the voters' right to know the candidates' criminal and financial antecedents is part of Art. 19(1)(a); Lily Thomas v UoI (2013) struck down s.8(4) of the RPA (immediate disqualification on conviction with 2 years or more); Public Interest Foundation v UoI (2019): directions on publishing criminal antecedents; and the Electoral Bonds Scheme was struck down in Association for Democratic Reforms v UoI (2024) [VERIFY].

sections.title: Nature, Incorporation and Types of Companies (Companies Act, 2013)
key_points: A company is an artificial juristic person with perpetual succession, a common seal (optional since 2015), the power to sue and be sued in its own name, and separate legal existence. Salomon v Salomon & Co (1897): a duly incorporated company is a separate legal entity distinct from its members, even a one-man company.

Section 2(20) 'company' means a company incorporated under the 2013 Act or any previous company law. Section 3: a company may be formed for any lawful purpose by 7 or more persons (public), 2 or more (private), or 1 person (One Person Company).

Private company (s.2(68)): restricts the right to transfer shares, limits members to 200 (excluding employees and ex-employees), prohibits invitation to the public to subscribe for securities; minimum paid-up capital requirement removed in 2015. Public company (s.2(71)): not a private company; minimum 7 members; no maximum; minimum 3 directors. (The earlier rule deeming a private company that is a subsidiary of a public company to be a public company was removed in 2015.)

One Person Company (s.2(62)): single member; nominee required; OPC can be a private company; threshold for mandatory conversion (paid-up capital Rs 50 lakh or turnover Rs 2 crore) was removed by the 2021 amendment rules, which also allow NRIs to form OPCs and cut the residency requirement to 120 days.

Small company (s.2(85)): paid-up capital up to Rs 4 crore and turnover up to Rs 40 crore originally; thresholds were later raised (Rs 10 crore and Rs 100 crore) [VERIFY]; exemption from certain filings. Section 8 company: for promoting charitable objects (commerce, art, science, sports, education, research, social welfare, religion, charity, protection of environment), with licence from the Central Government, income applied only to objects, no dividend. Producer company (Part IXA). Government company (s.2(45)): at least 51% paid-up share capital held by Central or State governments. Holding and subsidiary (s.2(46), 2(87)). Foreign company (s.2(42)). Dormant company (s.455). Listed company (s.2(52)).

Incorporation process: name approval (RUN, SPICe+ forms), Memorandum of Association (MoA; s.4), Articles of Association (AoA; s.5), declaration of compliance, DIN for directors, filing with the Registrar of Companies (ROC), and a Certificate of Incorporation (s.7), which is conclusive evidence of due incorporation. Company comes into existence from the date of incorporation mentioned in the certificate.

MoA clauses (public): name, registered office (state), objects, liability of members, authorised capital, and association clause (subscribers). AoA contains regulations for internal management; Table F is the model for companies limited by shares; the AoA is subordinate to the MoA and the Act; AoA can be altered by a special resolution (s.14), but cannot go beyond the MoA or the Act. Alteration of the name clause needs a special resolution and Central Government approval where applicable; objects clause by special resolution (and postal ballot for certain changes).

Promoters (s.2(69)): a person named in the prospectus or annual return, or who has control over affairs of the company, or on whose advice the Board is accustomed to act (professionals excluded). Promoters stand in a fiduciary position to the company: Erlanger v New Sombrero Phosphate Co (1878); Gluckstein v Barnes (1900): secret profits must be disclosed.

Prospectus (s.2(70), ss.26-40): any document described or issued as a prospectus including a red herring prospectus, shelf prospectus or any notice, circular, advertisement inviting offers from the public. Misstatement in a prospectus attracts civil liability (s.35) and criminal liability (s.34: fraud under s.447). Only public companies may issue prospectuses; private placement (s.42) cannot be offered to more than 200 persons in a financial year (excluding qualified institutional buyers and employees under ESOPs).

Share capital: equity and preference shares (s.43); issue at premium or discount (discount prohibited except sweat equity: s.53); allotment, calls, forfeiture and lien; buy-back (s.68): up to 25% of paid-up capital and free reserves, and not more than 25% of the total paid-up equity in a year; board resolution up to 10%; special resolution above that; debt-equity ratio 2:1 post buy-back; no re-issue of bought-back shares for 6 months [VERIFY]. Dematerialisation compulsory for listed companies; transfer of shares of private companies per AoA.

Dividend (s.123): paid out of profits of the year or accumulated profits after depreciation, and transfer to reserves; interim dividend allowed; unpaid dividend to be transferred to the Unpaid Dividend Account within 7 days of the 30-day period, and to the Investor Education and Protection Fund (IEPF) after 7 years (s.124-125).

sections.title: Doctrines: Lifting the Corporate Veil, Ultra Vires, Constructive Notice, Indoor Management, Majority Rule
key_points: Lifting the veil, statutory grounds: reducing members below statutory minimum (s.45 repealed; now in s.3), misdescription of the name, fraudulent trading (s.339), improper use of the name (s.12), liability for ultra vires prospectus misstatement, and holding-subsidiary consolidation. Judicial grounds: fraud or improper conduct (Gilford Motor Co v Horne, 1933; Jones v Lipman, 1962), sham or façade, determination of enemy character in wartime (Daimler Co v Continental Tyre, 1916), tax evasion (Juggilal Kamlapat v CIT, 1969), group enterprises (DHN Food Distributors v Tower Hamlets), and agency. Indian cases: State of UP v Renusagar Power Co (1988); Life Insurance Corporation of India v Escorts Ltd (1986): the veil may be lifted in the interest of justice and the public.

Doctrine of ultra vires: acts beyond the objects clause of the MoA are void and cannot be ratified even by all members. Ashbury Railway Carriage & Iron Co v Riche (1875). Acts within the powers of the company but beyond the powers of directors (intra vires the company) can be ratified. Acts beyond the AoA but within the MoA may be ratified.

Doctrine of constructive notice: every person dealing with a company is deemed to have read the MoA and AoA and the documents filed with the Registrar (Ernest v Nicholls). Doctrine of indoor management (rule in Royal British Bank v Turquand, 1856): outsiders dealing with a company in good faith may assume the internal procedures have been complied with. Exceptions: actual knowledge of irregularity; suspicion should have put one on inquiry (Anand Bihari Lal v Dinshaw & Co); forgery (Ruben v Great Fingall Consolidated, 1906); acts outside the apparent authority.

Doctrine of majority rule and minority protection: Foss v Harbottle (1843): the proper plaintiff for a wrong done to the company is the company itself; courts will not interfere in matters of internal management where the majority can ratify. Exceptions: ultra vires or illegal acts; fraud on the minority; acts requiring a special majority passed by simple majority; personal rights of members; just and equitable grounds. Statutory protection: oppression and mismanagement (ss.241-246), class action suits (s.245), and the right to apply for winding up.

Oppression and mismanagement (ss.241-242): any member may apply to the NCLT if the affairs of the company are being conducted in a manner prejudicial to public interest, oppressive to members, or prejudicial to the interests of the company; the facts must justify winding up on just and equitable grounds but winding up would unfairly prejudice the members. Eligibility to apply (s.244): for a company with share capital, at least 100 members or one-tenth of the total number of members, whichever is less, or members holding at least one-tenth of the issued share capital; the NCLT may waive these requirements. Powers: regulate affairs, buy-out, restrict transfer, set aside transactions, appoint directors.

Cyrus Investments Ltd v Tata Sons Ltd (2021): the Supreme Court set aside the NCLAT order restoring Cyrus Mistry; the removal of a director was valid; the 'oppression' standard was not met; the AoA's Articles 121 and 104 (conversion of public to private) were respected; reiterated that NCLT/NCLAT cannot rewrite company arrangements and that the test for oppression is 'burdensome, harsh and wrongful' conduct with a continuing course of acts. Also Needle Industries v Needle Industries Newey (1981).

Class action suit (s.245): members or depositors may file on behalf of the class against the company or its directors or auditors for acts prejudicial to interests; at least 100 members or 10% of the total members (or depositors) as the case may be.
