sections.title: Directors, Meetings, Resolutions, Audit, CSR, Fraud and Winding Up / Insolvency (IBC)
key_points: Directors (ss.149-172): minimum 3 for a public company, 2 for a private company, 1 for an OPC; maximum 15, extendable by special resolution; at least one woman director for prescribed classes of companies (listed companies and public companies with paid-up capital of Rs 100 crore or turnover Rs 300 crore); at least one director who stayed in India for not less than 182 days in the previous year (resident director); DIN is mandatory (s.153-154). Independent directors (s.149(6)): one-third of the Board for listed companies; tenure of 5 years renewable once by special resolution, then a cooling period of 3 years; they cannot receive stock options.

Disqualifications (s.164): unsound mind, undischarged insolvent, conviction for an offence involving moral turpitude with imprisonment of at least 6 months (5-year bar after release), disqualification by court order, failure to file financial statements or annual returns for 3 consecutive years, failure to repay deposits or debentures; Vacation of office (s.167). Removal of directors (s.169): by ordinary resolution with special notice; the director may make representations. Additional directors, nominee directors, alternate directors, and directors appointed in casual vacancy (s.161). Retirement by rotation (s.152): two-thirds of directors are subject to rotation and one-third retire every year.
Key Managerial Personnel (s.203): CEO/MD/manager, company secretary, whole-time director and CFO (applies to listed companies and public companies with paid-up capital Rs 10 crore or more).

Board meetings (s.173): at least 4 meetings a year with a gap of not more than 120 days between two consecutive meetings; first meeting within 30 days of incorporation; quorum: one-third of total strength or 2 directors, whichever is higher (s.174); notice of at least 7 days. Annual General Meeting (s.96): within 6 months of the financial year-end and not more than 15 months between two AGMs; first AGM within 9 months of the end of the first financial year; Registrar may extend by up to 3 months. EGM (s.100): requisition by members holding at least one-tenth of paid-up capital with voting rights. Quorum for general meetings (s.103): 5 members for public companies with up to 1,000 members, 15 for 1,000 to 5,000, and 30 for over 5,000; 2 members for private companies. Notice of at least 21 clear days (short notice with consent of 95% of members).

Resolutions: ordinary (simple majority of votes cast) and special (not less than 75% of votes cast; s.114). Matters requiring special resolution: alteration of AoA, change of name, alteration of objects, reduction of share capital, buy-back above 10%, appointment of a director beyond 15, etc. Postal ballot and e-voting are mandatory for listed companies for specified matters.

Related party transactions (s.188) need Board approval and, above prescribed thresholds, prior approval of the shareholders by ordinary resolution (after the 2017 amendment), with the related party abstaining from voting. Loans to directors (s.185): prohibited except in specified exceptions; with special resolution loans to entities in which directors are interested may be made for principal business [VERIFY post-2017 amendments]. Loans and investments by a company (s.186): up to 60% of paid-up capital, free reserves and securities premium, or 100% of free reserves and securities premium, whichever is higher; beyond that, special resolution.

Audit (ss.139-148): auditor appointed for a term of 5 years (renewable once for individuals up to 5 years; firms up to 10 years in two terms of 5 years); rotation after the term; cooling-off of 5 years; Cost audit for prescribed companies; Auditor's liability for misstatement (s.147). Section 143: powers and duties; reporting of fraud to the Central Government if above Rs 1 crore (and to the Audit Committee or Board if below Rs 1 crore). Removal of auditor: an auditor cannot be removed before the expiry of the term except by special resolution and Central Government approval (s.140). National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) is the audit regulator for listed and large companies.

CSR (s.135): applicable to companies with net worth of Rs 500 crore or more, or turnover of Rs 1,000 crore or more, or net profit of Rs 5 crore or more in any financial year; the Board must ensure spending of at least 2% of the average net profit of the immediately preceding three financial years; CSR Committee with at least 3 directors, including one independent director (not required for private companies with 2 directors); unspent amount to be transferred to an Unspent CSR Account (ongoing projects) or to a fund under Schedule VII (within 6 months of the end of the financial year) [VERIFY current wording]. The Companies (CSR Policy) Rules, 2014 were amended in 2021 and decriminalised partly (penal consequences are civil under the 2019/2020 amendments).

Fraud (s.447): any act, omission, concealment or abuse of position with intent to deceive, gain undue advantage or injure the interests of the company, shareholders, creditors or any other person, whether or not there is wrongful gain or loss. Punishment: imprisonment for 6 months to 10 years and fine of not less than the amount involved in the fraud, extending to 3 times that amount; if fraud involves public interest, minimum imprisonment is 3 years. The Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO, s.211) investigates. Bail for s.447 offences is subject to the twin conditions of s.212(6); Nikesh Tarachand Shah (2017) struck down the similar PMLA condition and the legislature later amended s.212(6) [VERIFY current position].

Decriminalisation: Companies (Amendment) Act 2019 and 2020 moved many compoundable offences to in-house adjudication; the Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act 2023 amended certain provisions; the Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Bill, 2025 proposes further decriminalisation of minor offences across various Acts [VERIFY status].

Tribunals: National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT; s.408) and NCLAT (s.410) constituted in 2016; appeals lie from the NCLT to the NCLAT within 45 days (s.421) and from the NCLAT to the Supreme Court within 60 days (s.423). Registrar of Companies (s.609 etc.) maintains the register; striking off defunct companies under s.248; shell company crackdown. Winding up of companies is by the NCLT (s.271): grounds include inability to pay debts, special resolution, acts against the sovereignty, integrity or security of the State, fraudulent conduct, default in filing financial statements for 5 consecutive years, and just and equitable grounds. Voluntary winding up is under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, s.59.

Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC): Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) can be initiated by a financial creditor (s.7), an operational creditor (s.9) or the corporate debtor itself (s.10) upon a default of at least Rs 1 crore (threshold raised from Rs 1 lakh in March 2020). Moratorium under s.14; interim resolution professional (IRP); Committee of Creditors (CoC) decides with 66% voting share; CIRP time limit 180 days, extendable by 90 days, with an overall outer limit of 330 days including litigation (Essar Steel (2019) read the outer limit as directory in exceptional cases; Ghanashyam Mishra and Sons v Edelweiss ARC (2021): once approved, the resolution plan binds all stakeholders including the Government and statutory dues of which no claim was filed); Section 29A bars ineligible persons (wilful defaulters, non-performing assets holders) from submitting resolution plans. Operational creditor trigger: Mobilox Innovations v Kirusa Software (2017): the existence of a pre-existing dispute defeats the s.9 application; Innoventive Industries v ICICI Bank (2017): existence of default is the key for the financial creditor; Swiss Ribbons v Union of India (2019): IBC held constitutional; Essar Steel India Ltd v Satish Kumar Gupta (2019): the commercial wisdom of the CoC is non-justiciable; the equality principle between creditors; Jaypee Kensington Boulevard Apartments Welfare Association v NBCC (2021): homebuyers are financial creditors; Pioneer Urban Land v UoI (2019). Pre-packaged insolvency (PPIRP) for MSMEs from 2021; Liquidation process under Chapter III; Personal guarantors: Lalit Kumar Jain v UoI (2021) upheld the notification extending IBC to personal guarantors.

AGM: within 6 months of year-end; max gap 15 months between AGMs.

sections.title: Members, Shareholders, Share Capital, Transfer of Shares, Debentures and Charges
key_points: Member vs shareholder: a 'member' (s.2(55)) is a subscriber to the memorandum, a person who agrees in writing to become a member and whose name is entered in the register of members, or a holder of shares whose name appears as a beneficial owner in the records of a depository. All shareholders are members; in a company limited by guarantee, there can be members without shares. Rights of members include the right to vote, receive dividends, inspect statutory registers (s.94, s.171), receive notices of meetings, requisition an EGM, apply for relief against oppression, and share in surplus assets on winding up.

Kinds of share capital (s.43): equity share capital (with voting rights, or with differential rights as to dividend, voting or otherwise per rules) and preference share capital (preferential right to dividend and return of capital on winding up). Preference shares must be redeemed within a maximum of 20 years (s.55); infrastructure companies may issue for longer than 20 years in specified cases. Irredeemable preference shares are prohibited. Cumulative, participating and convertible preference are the common varieties.

Types of capital: authorised (nominal) capital - maximum amount stated in the memorandum; issued capital; subscribed capital; called-up capital; paid-up capital; reserve capital (the uncalled amount that can be called only on winding up). Alteration of share capital (s.61) can be done by an ordinary resolution if the articles permit: increase of authorised capital, consolidation, sub-division, conversion of shares into stock, cancellation of unissued shares. Reduction of capital (s.66) requires a special resolution and NCLT confirmation (after notice to the Central Government, SEBI and creditors). Buy-back (s.68) is described in 4.11.

Allotment (s.39): the minimum subscription condition (90% under SEBI rules now) is applicable to public offers; shares must be allotted within the period permitted. Allotment of shares can be made only after the application money is received in a separate bank account; Return of allotment (PAS-3) within 30 days; share certificate to be issued within two months after allotment (s.56). An allotment is voidable at the option of the allottee if the prospectus is misleading. Irregular allotment may be set aside by the NCLT.

Calls on shares and forfeiture: the Articles (Table F) provide for calls; the Board makes calls with at least 14 days' notice; failure to pay allows forfeiture after notice (not less than 14 days); forfeited shares may be re-issued as fully paid for the amount paid; forfeiture must be in good faith and for the purpose for which it is authorised (Re Esparto Trading). A lien on partly paid shares is allowed in the articles for the company; for fully paid shares, a lien is allowed only in private companies by the articles; a public company's articles cannot give a lien over fully paid shares (Table F permits lien on partly paid shares only).

Transfer and transmission (ss.56, 58, 59): transfer requires an executed instrument of transfer (SH-4) accompanied by the share certificate and delivered to the company within 60 days of the date of execution; the company must register or refuse within 30 days. Refusal to register a transfer: in a private company, the articles may restrict transfer; in a public company, refusal is permitted only on the grounds set out in the Act and SEBI regulations; the aggrieved person may appeal to the NCLT within 30 days of refusal (s.58(3)). Transmission occurs by operation of law, for example death or insolvency of a member; the transmittee gets the same rights as the transferor. Listed securities are freely transferable (s.58(2) provision), and the securities of listed companies must be held in dematerialised form for transfer (from April 2019).

Rectification of register (s.59): the NCLT may order rectification where the name of a person is wrongly entered or omitted; an application can be made by the person aggrieved, any member, the company or the depository; the register of members is prima facie evidence of the matters directed or authorised to be inserted (s.44: shares are movable property transferable in the manner provided in the articles).

Share certificate and its estoppel effect: a certificate under the common seal (now sealed or signed by two directors and the company secretary) is prima facie evidence of title (s.46); the company is estopped from denying the statements in the certificate as against a bona fide purchaser who relied on it: Re Bahia and San Francisco Railway (1868); Ruben v Great Fingall Consolidated (1906) (forged certificate not binding).

Debentures (s.2(30), s.71): include debenture stock, bonds and other securities of a company whether constituting a charge on the assets of the company or not. They are debt instruments carrying interest; debenture-holders are creditors and not members, and have no voting rights. Secured debentures are those secured by a charge; debenture trust deed and a debenture trustee (SEBI-registered) must be appointed for an issue to the public, with a minimum number of subscribers; debentures with voting rights are prohibited (s.71(2)); the creation of a Debenture Redemption Reserve (DRR) and the deposit/investment of an amount in specified instruments (the 2019 rules exempted listed companies, with some conditions) [VERIFY]. A company may issue convertible debentures only if approved by special resolution (s.62(3)). Remedies of debenture holders: sue for principal and interest, appoint a receiver, enforce the charge, apply for winding up.

Charges (ss.77-87): a charge is an interest or lien created on the property or assets of a company or any of its undertakings as security, and includes a mortgage. Types: fixed (specific) charge; floating charge (on a class of assets present and future, which crystallises on default or winding up; Illingworth v Houldsworth (1904); Re Yorkshire Woolcombers Association (1903): characteristics); the floating charge allows the company to deal with the assets in the ordinary course of business until crystallisation. Registration: every charge created by a company must be registered with the Registrar within 30 days of creation (extendable by another 30 days on payment of additional fees, and thereafter by up to 300 days with the Registrar's condonation as per the 2019 amendment) [VERIFY]; an unregistered charge is void against the liquidator and any creditor of the company (s.77, s.78), though the debt remains payable; the company must also maintain a register of charges (s.85) and the charge-holder can file for registration (s.78). Satisfaction of charge must be filed (s.82). Registration of charges is also now available on the CERSAI (Central Registry of Securitisation Asset Reconstruction and Security Interest of India) for banks and financial institutions under the SARFAESI Act, 2002.

Preferential allotment, rights issue, bonus, ESOP and sweat equity: further issue of shares (s.62): a rights issue offers the shares to existing shareholders in proportion; the offer remains open for 15 days (reduced to 7 days by the 2020 SEBI/MCA relaxation for rights issues) [VERIFY]; a preferential allotment requires a special resolution and compliance with pricing rules (private placement offer letter s.42 and Rule 14). Bonus shares are issued out of free reserves, securities premium or capital redemption reserve (s.63) and must be authorised by the articles; they cannot be issued in lieu of dividend. Employee stock options require special resolution (s.62(1)(b)). Sweat equity shares (s.54): issued at a discount or for consideration other than cash to directors or employees for know-how or intellectual property rights; to be issued after one year of commencement of business and by special resolution (start-ups: 10 years).

Securities premium account (s.52): premium amount must be credited and may be applied only for purposes such as issuing fully paid bonus shares, writing off preliminary expenses, writing off commission or discount on issue of shares or debentures, providing for the premium payable on redemption of redeemable preference shares or debentures, and buy-back of shares. Capital redemption reserve account (s.69): on buy-back out of free reserves or securities premium, an amount equal to the nominal value of the shares bought must be transferred to the CRR.

Prohibition on financial assistance for purchase of own shares (s.67): a public company cannot give financial assistance for the purchase of its own shares or those of its holding company, except for employee share schemes (in trust for employees) and loans to employees (up to six months' salary). Prohibition on holding of own shares through a subsidiary (s.19): a subsidiary company cannot hold shares in its holding company; allotment or transfer to a subsidiary is void; Cross-holding rules. Preference share dividend must be paid before equity dividend.

Subscribers and 'inspection': the register of members (s.88), index of members, register of debenture-holders, and register of other security holders; Annual return (s.92) is to be filed within 60 days of the AGM; the register of significant beneficial owners (s.90): an individual who holds, directly or indirectly, at least 10% of shares or voting rights (or exercises significant influence or control) must file a declaration within 90 days; Rule in the Companies (Significant Beneficial Owners) Rules, 2018.

An unregistered charge is void against the liquidator and the creditors, but the debt itself is not extinguished.

sections.title: Directors' Duties, Powers, Remuneration, Related Party and Governance (ss.166-197, 177-179)
key_points: Fiduciary character of directors: they are agents, trustees (of the company's property) and managing partners. Duties under s.166 (statutory codification): (1) act in accordance with the articles; (2) act in good faith to promote the objects of the company for the benefit of its members as a whole and in the best interests of the company, its employees, the shareholders, the community and for the protection of the environment; (3) exercise duties with due and reasonable care, skill and diligence, and independent judgment; (4) not to be involved in a situation in which he may have a direct or indirect interest that conflicts, or possibly may conflict, with the interest of the company; (5) not to achieve or attempt to achieve any undue gain or advantage either to himself or to his relatives, partners or associates (if found guilty, he is liable to pay an amount equal to the gain to the company); (6) not to assign his office, and any such assignment is void. Penalty for contravention: fine from Rs 1 lakh to Rs 5 lakh (s.166(7)).

Case law on duties: Regal (Hastings) Ltd v Gulliver (1942): directors who made profit from an opportunity arising out of their position must account for it; Cook v Deeks (1916): directors cannot divert a business opportunity from the company; Percival v Wright (1902): directors owe duties to the company, not individual shareholders (but a fiduciary duty may arise in special circumstances); Re City Equitable Fire Insurance Co (1925): duty of care and skill is judged by the director's knowledge and experience, with no guarantee of mistakes; Foss v Harbottle: breach of duty is a wrong to the company.

Powers of the Board (s.179): the Board is entitled to exercise all such powers and to do all such acts as the company is authorised to exercise, except those that the Act requires to be exercised in general meeting. Certain powers can be exercised only by Board resolution at its meeting (not by circulation): to make calls on shareholders, issue securities including debentures, borrow money, invest funds, grant loans or give guarantee or provide security, approve financial statements and the Board's report, diversify the business, approve amalgamation, merger or reconstruction, take over a company or acquire a controlling or substantial stake in another, and make political contributions.

Restrictions on Board powers (s.180) - the following require a special resolution: (a) selling, leasing or otherwise disposing of the whole or substantially the whole of an undertaking of the company (substantially the whole means 20% or more of the value of the undertaking); (b) investing the compensation received on compulsory acquisition; (c) borrowing money in excess of the aggregate of paid-up share capital, free reserves and securities premium (temporary loans from bankers in the ordinary course are excluded); (d) remitting or giving time for repayment of any debt due from a director. The company's ultra vires borrowing is void; lenders with notice of the lack of authority cannot enforce it.

Managerial remuneration (s.197, Schedule V): total managerial remuneration to the directors, including managing director, whole-time directors and manager, must not exceed 11% of the net profits of the company; if no or inadequate profits, remuneration is payable as per Schedule V with the approval of the shareholders and, where required, the Central Government (now delegated by the 2017 amendments to shareholders through a special resolution). Independent directors may receive only sitting fees, profit-related commission as approved, and reimbursement of expenses; they cannot receive stock options.

Contracts with related parties (s.188): a company cannot enter into specified transactions with a related party (sale, purchase or supply of goods or materials, selling or disposing of property, leasing property, availing or rendering of services, appointment of any agent for purchase or sale, appointment to an office or place of profit, underwriting the subscription of securities) except with the consent of the Board by a resolution at a meeting; for transactions exceeding the prescribed thresholds, prior approval of the company by a resolution (an ordinary resolution after the 2017 amendment) is required, with the related parties not voting. Transactions between a holding company and its wholly owned subsidiary are exempt from the shareholder approval; arm's length transactions in the ordinary course of business are exempt from the Board and shareholder approval requirements of s.188(1) (but not for listed companies under SEBI LODR). Contravention can be avoided by the company if the contract is entered into with a director or his relative who has not obtained the consent; the director concerned is liable to indemnify the company.

Disclosure of interest (s.184): every director must disclose his concern or interest in any company or companies, bodies corporate, firms or other associations of individuals at the first meeting of the Board in which he participates as a director and thereafter at the first meeting of the Board in every financial year or whenever there is a change in the disclosures. An interested director must not participate in the discussion or vote on the matter (except in a private company where the articles do not forbid it, and subject to certain conditions). A contract in which a director is interested and which is not disclosed can be avoided by the company.

Loans to directors and others (ss.185-186): s.185 prohibits a company from advancing any loan, including any loan represented by a book debt, or giving any guarantee or providing any security in connection with a loan taken by a director or by any other person in whom the director is interested, subject to exceptions (e.g., loans to a managing or whole-time director as part of the conditions of service, loans to a wholly owned subsidiary, loans to a body corporate in which the director is interested, if approved by a special resolution and used by the borrower for its principal business activities, at a rate of interest not less than the prevailing yield on government securities of comparable tenure). A contravention is punishable with a fine of Rs 5 lakh to Rs 25 lakh and the director or other person to whom the loan is given with imprisonment up to six months or a fine of Rs 5 lakh to Rs 25 lakh. Section 186 limits loans, guarantees and investments to 60% of paid-up share capital, free reserves and securities premium or 100% of free reserves and securities premium, whichever is more, unless the special resolution is passed; no loan can be given at a rate of interest lower than the prevailing yield of government securities.

Committees: Audit Committee (s.177): mandatory for listed companies and public companies meeting the prescribed thresholds; at least three directors with independent directors forming a majority; the chairperson and majority of the members should be able to read and understand financial statements; functions include recommending appointment and remuneration of auditors, review of financial statements and related party transactions, scrutiny of inter-corporate loans, valuation of undertakings, and evaluation of internal financial controls; a vigil mechanism (whistle-blower policy) is mandatory for listed companies and companies accepting deposits or borrowing above prescribed amounts (s.177(9)). Nomination and Remuneration Committee (s.178): three or more non-executive directors, at least half independent; Stakeholders Relationship Committee for companies having more than 1,000 shareholders, debenture holders, deposit holders and other security holders; CSR Committee (s.135) as above.

Officer in default (s.2(60)): any whole-time director, key managerial personnel, or where there are none, such director as specified by the Board (and where the Board specifies none, all directors), any person in accordance with whose directions or instructions the Board is accustomed to act, and certain other persons (company secretary, share transfer agents, etc.) who are in default of statutory requirements. Section 447 and other penal sections impose liability on officers in default. Independent and non-executive directors are liable only for acts or omissions that occurred with their knowledge, attributable through Board processes, and with their consent or connivance or where they have not acted diligently (s.149(12)).

Secretarial audit and corporate social responsibility: secretarial audit (s.204) applies to listed companies and other prescribed companies, and a practising company secretary conducts it; the Board's Report must include the secretarial audit report, CSR report, risk management, declaration by independent directors and the directors' responsibility statement (s.134(5)). Maintenance of registers, annual return (s.92) within 60 days of the AGM, and financial statements (s.129; Schedule III) laid before the AGM and filed within 30 days of the AGM (s.137). A defaulting company and each officer in default are liable to penalty. The Companies Act has a graded penalty structure with in-house adjudication under s.454 for civil penalties and compounding (s.441).

Independent directors cannot get stock options.

sections.title: Mergers, Amalgamation, Compromise and Arrangement; Winding Up; NCLT/NCLAT; Registrar and Striking Off
key_points: Compromise or arrangement (ss.230-232): a company, its creditors, or its members may propose a compromise or arrangement; the NCLT directs a meeting of the creditors or class of creditors or members; the scheme must be approved by a majority in number representing three-fourths in value of the creditors, or class of creditors, or members, present and voting in person, by proxy or by postal ballot; once sanctioned by the NCLT, it is binding on all creditors/members and on the company. Notice to the Central Government, Income Tax authorities, RBI, SEBI, Registrar, stock exchanges, the Competition Commission of India and other sectoral regulators; objections by persons holding 10% or more of shareholding or having outstanding debt exceeding 5% of the total outstanding debt are permitted for the scheme.

Fast-track merger (s.233): between two or more small companies, or between a holding company and its wholly owned subsidiary, or other prescribed classes, with approval of the Regional Director (Central Government), without NCLT; requires the consent of 90% of the shareholders in value and 90% of the creditors in value; Registrar and Official Liquidator objections to be considered. Cross-border mergers are permitted under s.234 with prior RBI approval.

Amalgamation concepts: amalgamation (merger of one or more companies into another, or of two or more companies to form a new company), absorption, reconstruction. Tax-neutral under s.2(1B) of the Income Tax Act where specified conditions are fulfilled. Competition law: the Competition Act, 2002 (ss.5-6, 20) requires notification of combinations above the prescribed thresholds; the Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023 introduced the deal value threshold of Rs 2,000 crore. Take-overs of listed companies are governed by the SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011: an acquirer must make an open offer on acquiring 25% or more voting rights or on acquiring control; a creeping acquisition limit of 5% per financial year for those holding between 25% and 75%.

Winding up: modes - (a) by the Tribunal (compulsory); (b) voluntary winding up (now under IBC for solvent companies: s.59 IBC); (c) winding up subject to supervision of the Tribunal (omitted in 2013 Act). Grounds for winding up by the Tribunal (s.271): (a) the company is unable to pay its debts; (b) the company has by special resolution resolved that it be wound up by the Tribunal; (c) the company has acted against the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India, the security of the State, friendly relations with foreign states, public order, decency or morality; (d) [the sick-company ground is no longer operative]; (e) on an application by the Registrar or any other person authorised by the Central Government, that the affairs of the company have been conducted in a fraudulent manner or the company was formed for fraudulent and unlawful purposes or persons concerned in the formation or management of its affairs have been guilty of fraud, misfeasance or misconduct; (f) the company has made a default in filing with the Registrar its financial statements or annual returns for immediately preceding five consecutive financial years; (g) the Tribunal is of the opinion that it is just and equitable that the company be wound up. Deemed inability to pay debts (s.271(2)): creditor to whom the company owes more than Rs 1 lakh has served a notice in writing and the company has failed to pay within three weeks.

Who can petition for winding up (s.272): the company, a creditor (including contingent or prospective), a contributory, all or any of the above, the Registrar, or a person authorised by the Central Government in the case of public interest grounds; the Central Government or a State Government for the sovereignty/morality ground. Just and equitable ground examples: deadlock in a quasi-partnership (Ebrahimi v Westbourne Galleries, 1973: the company's formation based on mutual confidence and the exclusion of a member from management justifies winding up); loss of substratum (Re German Date Coffee Co, 1882); fraud on minority; oppression.

Consequences and process: the Tribunal appoints an Official Liquidator or a company liquidator from a panel; once the winding-up order is made, there is a stay of suits against the company, restrictions on dispositions and share transfers after the order, and the Board's powers cease; the liquidator takes custody of assets, settles the list of contributories, and makes calls; the order in which debts are paid follows s.326 (overriding preferential payments): first the costs and expenses; workmen's dues and secured creditors rank pari passu; followed by employees' dues, then the Central and State Government dues; then unsecured creditors, then preference shareholders and equity shareholders. Fraudulent preference (s.328), transfers of property within one year before the commencement of winding up being void (s.329) and the offences by officers of the company in liquidation (s.339 fraudulent trading, s.340 misconduct) are tested.

Insolvency vs winding up: for insolvent companies, the IBC prevails (s.238 IBC overrides inconsistent laws: Innoventive Industries; the liquidation process under Chapter III of Part II of the IBC replaces compulsory winding up for insolvency). The Companies Act winding-up regime remains for non-insolvency grounds (sovereignty, fraud, default in filing returns, etc.). Pending winding-up petitions against the company in which notice has not been served could be transferred to NCLT under the 2016 notification.

NCLT and NCLAT: constituted under s.408 and s.410; NCLT has the principal bench in New Delhi and benches across India; powers include oppression and mismanagement, rectification of registers, reduction of capital, schemes of arrangement, winding up, investigation orders; the Tribunal has the powers of a civil court under the CPC (s.424) and can punish contempt. Appeals from the NCLT to the NCLAT (s.421) within 45 days (extendable by another 45 days); appeals from the NCLAT to the Supreme Court (s.423) within 60 days on any question of law. Under IBC, appeals from NCLT to NCLAT lie within 30 days extendable by 15 days (s.61), and to the Supreme Court within 45 days (s.62). The Supreme Court in Union of India v R. Gandhi (2010) held that the creation of the Tribunal is valid if the technical members have judicial competence; Madras Bar Association v UoI (2014, 2020) struck down parts of the Tribunal Rules and the 2017 Finance Act provisions on tribunal appointments [VERIFY].

Registrar of Companies and defunct companies: the ROC (s.609) maintains the register, receives documents, and may inspect the company's books (s.206). Striking off the name of a defunct company (s.248): the Registrar may strike off the name if the company has not commenced business within one year of incorporation, or has not carried on business or operations for two immediately preceding financial years and has not applied for dormant status; the company, its directors and members, and creditors can apply to the NCLT within three years for restoration (s.252); Rule: the liability of directors continues even after striking off (s.250). Shell company: a company is generally viewed as a shell if it has no active business, no significant accounting transactions or assets; the Government's 2017 crackdown led to the disqualification of roughly 3.5 lakh directors under s.164(2)(a) [VERIFY figures and litigation]. A company can apply for dormant status (s.455) if it is inactive.

Investigation (ss.210-229): the Central Government may order an investigation by the Registrar or an inspector on the report of the Registrar, on a special resolution or Tribunal order, in public interest, or by the SFIO (s.212), when the affairs of the company need to be investigated in public interest or by a special resolution. The SFIO under the Ministry of Corporate Affairs is a multi-disciplinary body that takes up serious fraud; offences under s.447 are cognizable and bailable only subject to twin conditions in s.212(6) as amended; the Supreme Court in Nikesh Tarachand Shah v UoI (2017) struck down the twin condition of PMLA s.45 (which was later restored by the 2018 amendment and upheld in Vijay Madanlal Choudhary v UoI, 2022). The SFIO's powers of arrest under s.212(8): the Director, Additional Director or Assistant Director can arrest with reasons recorded [VERIFY].

sections.title: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016: CIRP, Moratorium, Waterfall, Avoidance Transactions, Landmark Cases
key_points: Object and structure: the IBC consolidates laws on insolvency of corporate persons, partnership firms and individuals, in a time-bound manner, to maximise value of assets, promote entrepreneurship, availability of credit and balance the interests of all stakeholders. Regulator: the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI). Adjudicating authority: NCLT for corporate persons; Debt Recovery Tribunal for individuals and partnership firms. Information Utilities (IUs) store financial information to establish default. Insolvency Professionals (IPs) conduct the process. The Code has a non-obstante clause overriding other laws (s.238).

Initiation of CIRP: by a financial creditor (s.7), by an operational creditor after a demand notice (s.8-9), or by the corporate applicant (s.10), on default of at least Rs 1 crore. Financial creditor: a person to whom a financial debt is owed (disbursed against consideration for the time value of money), including allottees of real estate projects (explanation to s.5(8)(f)); the 2020 amendment to s.7 requires a minimum of 100 allottees or 10% of allottees in the same real estate project, whichever is less, to file a joint application; operational creditor: a person to whom an operational debt (claim arising from provision of goods or services, including employment or a debt in respect of the repayment of dues arising under any law, payable to the Central Government, any State Government or any local authority) is owed. Demand notice (s.8) gives 10 days to the debtor to repay or to bring notice of a dispute; s.9 application is filed on failure; the NCLT must admit or reject within 14 days of the application.

Admission and consequences: for a s.7 application, the NCLT must be satisfied that a default has occurred and the application is complete; the NCLT gives the debtor an opportunity to be heard (Innoventive: once default and completeness are shown, the application must be admitted; Vidarbha Industries Power Ltd v Axis Bank Ltd (2022): admission is not automatic, the NCLT has discretion to consider whether the debtor is viable). Upon admission: moratorium (s.14) prohibits institution or continuation of suits or proceedings against the corporate debtor, transferring, encumbering or alienating its assets, any action to foreclose, recover or enforce any security interest, and recovery of property by an owner or lessor; supply of essential goods and services cannot be terminated; Interim Resolution Professional (IRP) takes over the management; the board of directors is suspended; public announcement inviting claims (s.15); the Committee of Creditors (CoC) is constituted of financial creditors (s.21) with voting shares in proportion to the financial debt; operational creditors do not have voting rights but may attend.

Timeline: CIRP must be completed within 180 days, extendable by 90 days by the NCLT (s.12), with a maximum of 330 days including litigation and extension (inserted in 2019); Essar Steel (2019) read the 330-day outer limit as directory in exceptional circumstances; the 2019 amendment again inserted the 330-day limit with a time for exclusion of litigation delays [VERIFY]. Resolution plan (s.30): submitted by a resolution applicant; must provide for payment of CIRP costs in priority, payment to operational creditors (not less than the amount receivable in the liquidation), repayment to financial creditors who dissent (not less than the liquidation value); approved by the CoC by a vote of not less than 66% of the voting share (reduced from 75% in 2019) and then approved by the NCLT (s.31); it binds the corporate debtor, its employees, members, creditors, guarantors and other stakeholders (Ghanashyam Mishra and Sons Pvt Ltd v Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Co (2021): a successful resolution plan extinguishes all claims not part of the plan: the 'clean slate' principle). Withdrawal after admission (s.12A): permitted with the approval of 90% voting share of the CoC (Uttara Foods and Feeds v Mona Pharmacem, 2019; Brilliant Alloys v Mahadeo Prasad Chhawsaria (2018): not the NCLT's discretion alone).

Section 29A (ineligibility of resolution applicants): persons who are undischarged insolvents, wilful defaulters, persons whose account has been classified as an NPA for one year or more (unless they pay off all overdue amounts), persons convicted for offences punishable with imprisonment for two years or more (except for certain offences), persons disqualified as directors, persons prohibited by SEBI, persons who have executed a guarantee for a corporate debtor under CIRP or liquidation where the guarantee has been invoked and remains unpaid, or related parties of any such persons. ArcelorMittal India Pvt Ltd v Satish Kumar Gupta (2019): the 'connected person' and the date for determining NPA; Chitra Sharma v Union of India (2018): Jaypee Infratech homebuyers' rights and s.29A's purposes.

Waterfall under liquidation (s.53): (1) insolvency resolution process costs and liquidation costs; (2) workmen's dues for the 24 months preceding the liquidation commencement date and debts owed to secured creditors who have relinquished their security (pari passu); (3) wages and unpaid dues to employees other than workmen for the 12 months preceding; (4) financial debts owed to unsecured creditors; (5) amount due to the Central and State Governments for the 2 years preceding the liquidation commencement date and debts owed to secured creditors for any amount unpaid following enforcement of security interest; (6) remaining debts and dues; (7) preference shareholders; (8) equity shareholders or partners. The Supreme Court in Essar Steel (2019) held that the CoC has the commercial wisdom to distribute proceeds among creditors in a resolution plan and that the equality principle does not require equal treatment of unequals (financial and operational creditors); the decision protected the secured creditors' priority.

Avoidance transactions (ss.43-51, 66): the resolution professional or liquidator can apply to the NCLT to avoid: preferential transactions (within 2 years if made to related parties, within 1 year otherwise, before the insolvency commencement date), undervalued transactions (same look-back periods), extortionate credit transactions (within 2 years), and fraudulent or wrongful trading (s.66): where the business of the corporate debtor has been carried on with intent to defraud creditors or for any fraudulent purpose, the persons who were knowingly parties may be made liable to contribute to the assets. Anuj Jain, Interim Resolution Professional for Jaypee Infratech Ltd v Axis Bank Ltd (2020): the Court upheld the avoidance of mortgage transactions entered into by Jaypee Infratech in favour of lenders for the benefit of its holding company, as undervalued/preferential transactions.

Landmark decisions: Mobilox Innovations Pvt Ltd v Kirusa Software (2017): the test for pre-existing dispute: whether there is a plausible contention requiring further investigation, which is not patently feeble; Macquarie Bank Ltd v Shilpi Cable Technologies (2017): the operational creditor's demand notice must be served in the prescribed form, and the dispute may be raised in response; Swiss Ribbons Pvt Ltd v UoI (2019): upheld the constitutionality of IBC, including the differential treatment of financial and operational creditors, s.29A and the CoC's role; K. Sashidhar v Indian Overseas Bank (2019): CoC's commercial wisdom is non-justiciable, including a decision on liquidation vs resolution; Committee of Creditors of Essar Steel India Ltd v Satish Kumar Gupta (2019): CoC decision on distribution is final; Jaypee Kensington (2021): protection of the interests of homebuyers; B.K. Educational Services v Parag Gupta (2018): the Limitation Act, 1963 applies to IBC applications (3 years from the date of default; Article 137); Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Ltd v Amit Gupta (2021): the NCLT cannot adjudicate on the termination of a contract by the counterparty under the contract on the ground of insolvency unless the contract is of the type central to the corporate debtor's survival (Section 60(5)); Lalit Kumar Jain v UoI (2021): the personal guarantors to corporate debtors can be proceeded against even after approval of the resolution plan; Dena Bank v C. Shivakumar Reddy (2021): the application of Article 137; Kotak Mahindra Bank v A. Balakrishnan (2022): the acknowledgement in the balance sheet extends limitation.

Pre-packaged insolvency (Chapter III-A, inserted in April 2021): available only to MSMEs, with a threshold of default of Rs 10 lakh, initiated by the corporate debtor with approval of 66% of the financial creditors that are not related parties, and with a time limit of 120 days for the process; the existing management stays in control (debtor-in-possession model). Fast-track CIRP: for corporate debtors with assets or income below Rs 1 crore, startups and unlisted companies, with 90 days (extendable by 45 days). Group insolvency and cross-border insolvency are under discussion; the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (Amendment) Bill, 2025 (if passed) introduces creditor-initiated insolvency resolution and group insolvency frameworks [VERIFY status].

Personal insolvency (Part III): fresh start process (for debts up to Rs 35,000, as notified), insolvency resolution process for individuals and firms (Part III, Chapter III) and bankruptcy (Chapter IV); personal guarantors to corporate debtors fall under the DRT jurisdiction from 1 December 2019 notification, upheld in Lalit Kumar Jain. Liquidation of the corporate debtor: the liquidator is appointed (s.34), and the liquidation process must be completed within two years (regulation 44 of the IBBI Liquidation Regulations); sale of the corporate debtor as a going concern is encouraged. Offences under the Code: concealment of property (s.69), transactions defrauding creditors (s.69), misconduct in the course of insolvency (s.70), falsification of books (s.71), false representations to creditors (s.73), contravention of moratorium (s.74), punished with imprisonment from 3 to 5 years and fines [VERIFY].

sections.title: Other Business Forms and Corporate Governance: LLP Act 2008, Producer Companies, SEBI and Listed Companies
key_points: Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008: an LLP is a body corporate with a separate legal entity from its partners, perpetual succession, the ability to own property and to sue and be sued. Minimum two partners; no maximum; at least two designated partners who are individuals, of whom at least one must be a resident in India (stayed for at least 120 days in the preceding year) [VERIFY]. Partners' liability is limited to their agreed contribution; no partner is liable for the wrongful acts or omissions of any other partner (s.28); but liability for fraud: the LLP and the partners who acted with intent to defraud are liable without limit (s.30). Every partner is an agent of the LLP, not of other partners (s.26). Registration with the Registrar through the incorporation document (s.11); the LLP agreement governs mutual rights and duties; in the absence of an agreement, the First Schedule applies (equal sharing of profits, no remuneration, etc.). Conversion of a partnership firm, private company or unlisted public company into an LLP (ss.55-58). The LLP Act (s.67) provides that the provisions of the Partnership Act, 1932 do not apply; the Central Government may apply provisions of the Companies Act to LLPs by notification.

Producer companies (Part IXA of the Companies Act, 1956, continued): body corporate of primary producers (farmers) with a minimum of ten individuals or two producer institutions; members' liability limited by shares; at least five and not more than fifteen directors; one member one vote in principle; restrictions on transfer of shares; profits distributed through patronage bonus and limited dividend. Nidhi companies (s.406): Nidhi Rules 2014: mutual benefit societies accepting deposits from and lending to members only, with 200 members and Rs 10 lakh net-owned funds at least [VERIFY]. Section 8 companies as described above. Sole proprietorship and partnership (Indian Partnership Act, 1932) are not corporate bodies: the partnership firm has no separate legal personality.

Corporate governance and SEBI: Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992 (SEBI as a statutory regulator since 1992): functions include protecting investors, regulating the securities market and promoting its development; SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 (LODR) require listed companies to ensure a minimum of one-third independent directors (if the chairman is non-executive and a promoter, one-half), at least one woman director, a separate meeting of independent directors, a minimum of 4 board meetings a year, an audit committee, a nomination and remuneration committee, a stakeholders relationship committee, a risk management committee for the top 1,000 listed entities, a whistle-blower policy, and related-party transaction approvals. Insider trading is regulated by the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015: trading by an insider while in possession of unpublished price sensitive information (UPSI); the code of conduct for fair disclosure. Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956 regulates stock exchanges and contracts in securities. Depositories Act, 1996 provides for dematerialisation.

Sahara India Real Estate Corp Ltd v SEBI (2012): Optionally Fully Convertible Debentures (OFCDs) issued to millions of investors were 'securities' and public issue; Sahara was ordered to refund the money. National Stock Exchange (co-location) cases: SEBI's penal orders against NSE and its officers. For AIBE, understand SEBI's three functions (quasi-legislative, quasi-judicial, quasi-executive), appeals to the Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT) within 45 days and then to the Supreme Court (s.15Z of the SEBI Act).

Competition Act, 2002: the Competition Commission of India (CCI) regulates anti-competitive agreements (s.3), abuse of dominant position (s.4) and combinations (ss.5-6); the 2023 amendment introduced settlement and commitment mechanisms, leniency plus, and the deal value threshold of Rs 2,000 crore (where the target has substantial business operations in India). Competition Appellate Tribunal: NCLAT hears appeals from the CCI (since 2017). Case: CCI v Coordination Committee of Artistes and Technicians of West Bengal Film and Television (2017); Excel Crop Care v CCI (2017) on penalty and turnover (relevant turnover).

special_laws_snapshot.law: Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 (as amended 2015 and 2018)
key_points: Section 3 lists atrocities committed by a person who is not a member of an SC or ST against a member of an SC or ST: forcing to eat inedible substances, dumping excreta, parading naked, wrongful occupation of land, compelling to do forced labour, denial of access to water, sexual exploitation, and others; punishment generally 6 months to 5 years and fine; s.3(2)(v): offence under IPC punishable with 10 years or more against a member of an SC/ST knowing him to be so, punishable with imprisonment for life and fine; s.3(1)(r) and (s): intentional insult or abuse in any place within public view.

Anticipatory bail is barred (s.18); the Supreme Court in Subhash Kashinath Mahajan v State of Maharashtra (2018) diluted the provisions (preliminary inquiry, approval for arrest of public servants), but Parliament restored the original position by the 2018 Amendment (s.18A) and the Supreme Court upheld the amendment in Prathvi Raj Chauhan v Union of India (2020); Hitesh Verma v State of Uttarakhand (2020): the insult must occur 'within public view' and the 'place within public view' is an open place seen or heard by the public.

Special Courts and Exclusive Special Courts; speedy trial; relief and rehabilitation; the offence is non-compoundable though the courts have quashed on settlement in suitable cases under inherent powers [VERIFY].

'Public servant' defined in s.2(c); s.7: public servant taking undue advantage: 3 to 7 years and fine; s.7A: taking undue advantage to influence a public servant by corrupt or illegal means: 3 to 7 years; s.8: giving or promising to give undue advantage to a public servant: up to 7 years or fine or both (a bribe-giver is also liable); s.9: offence relating to bribing a public servant by a commercial organisation; s.13: criminal misconduct by a public servant (now confined to dishonest or fraudulent misappropriation of property entrusted and disproportionate assets): 4 to 10 years and fine; s.17A: prior approval of the competent authority is necessary for an inquiry or investigation into an offence alleged to have been committed by a public servant in relation to a recommendation or decision in discharge of official functions (not for cases of arrest on the spot on a charge of accepting or attempting to accept undue advantage).

Sanction for prosecution (s.19): required for taking cognizance against a public servant; Subramanian Swamy v Manmohan Singh (2012): the sanction should be decided within three months (four with the Attorney General's advice); Neeraj Dutta v State (Govt of NCT of Delhi) (2022): a Constitution Bench held that a demand and acceptance of illegal gratification can be proved by circumstantial evidence in the absence of direct evidence if the complainant turns hostile or dies; the Supreme Court in State of Telangana v Managipet (2019) discussed the effect of the 2018 amendment on proof of demand [VERIFY]. P. Satyanarayana Murthy v State of AP (2015): proof of demand is indispensable for s.7 and s.13(1)(d).

Defines 'unlawful activity', 'terrorist act' (s.15), 'terrorist organisation' (First Schedule), and 'unlawful association' (s.2(p)); punishments for raising funds for terrorist acts (s.17), conspiracy (s.18), membership of a terrorist organisation (s.38) and support (s.39). Bail is restricted by s.43D(5): the court cannot grant bail if there are reasonable grounds for believing that the accusation against the person is prima facie true (NIA v Zahoor Ahmad Shah Watali, 2019; contrast Union of India v K.A. Najeeb (2021): constitutional courts can grant bail where there is prolonged incarceration and the trial is unlikely to conclude soon; Vernon v State of Maharashtra (2023): a prima facie standard for ss.15, 17 and 18 requires specific evidence; Thwaha Fasal v UoI (2021); Gurwinder Singh v State of Punjab (2024): upheld the Watali approach in a restrictive way) [VERIFY].

Overlap with BNS s.113 (terrorist act): police officers of the rank of Superintendent of Police have the discretion whether to proceed under BNS s.113 or UAPA; the Supreme Court has held that the UAPA, as a special law, prevails to the extent of inconsistency. Arup Bhuyan: mere membership is not an offence for a banned organisation unless active involvement is shown (2011); the Government's review of that reading-down was heard by a larger Bench in 2023 [VERIFY outcome].

special_laws_snapshot.law: Arms Act, 1959 and Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956 and Indecent Representation of Women (Prohibition) Act, 1986
key_points: Arms Act s.25: possession of prohibited arms or ammunition without licence: 3 to 7 years and fine (s.25(1A)); s.27: use of arms: 3 to 7 years for use of arms or ammunition in contravention of s.5, and death or life imprisonment if the use results in death (s.27(3) mandatory death penalty struck down in State of Punjab v Dalbir Singh, 2012). Possession of a firearm in a public place without licence (e.g., in a car) attracts both the Arms Act and BNS provisions.

ITPA 1956: punishes keeping a brothel (s.3), living on the earnings of prostitution (s.4), procuring or inducing for prostitution (s.5), detaining a person in premises where prostitution is carried on (s.6), prostitution in or near public places (s.7), seducing or soliciting for purposes of prostitution (s.8); trafficking is now under BNS s.143; Gaurav Jain v Union of India (1997); Budhadev Karmaskar v State of West Bengal (2011; 2022): sex workers have a right to dignity under Art. 21 and police must not harass adult consenting sex workers (2022 directions).

Indecent Representation of Women (Prohibition) Act: prohibits publication or distribution of indecent representation of women through advertisements, publications, writings, paintings, figures or in any other manner; punishment up to 2 years and fine of Rs 2,000 to Rs 5,000 for first conviction; 2 to 7 years and fine of Rs 10,000 to Rs 1 lakh for subsequent convictions.

special_laws_snapshot.law: Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015
key_points: Child in conflict with law (below 18); heinous offences (minimum punishment seven years or more), serious offences (3 to 7 years), petty offences (up to 3 years); preliminary assessment by the Juvenile Justice Board for a child aged 16-18 who commits a heinous offence, covering mental and physical capacity, ability to understand the consequences, and the circumstances; the Board may then transfer the case to the Children's Court for trial as an adult; the maximum stay in a place of safety is up to age 21; death penalty and life imprisonment without release are prohibited (s.21); records are to be destroyed after the completion of the appeal period (s.24: removal of disqualification attached to conviction).

Age determination (s.94): matriculation certificate or equivalent, birth certificate from school, or birth certificate from a corporation, municipal authority or panchayat; in the absence of these, ossification test or other latest medical age determination test; Jarnail Singh v State of Haryana (2013): the same rule applies to child victims; Ashwani Kumar Saxena v State of MP (2012); Pratap Singh v State of Jharkhand (2005): the relevant date for determining juvenility is the date of the offence; Hari Ram v State of Rajasthan (2009). Juvenility claim may be raised at any stage, even after final disposal (s.9(2); Abuzar Hossain v State of WB, 2012).

special_laws_snapshot.law: Prevention of Damage to Public Property Act, 1984 and Mob-Violence Jurisprudence
key_points: Section 3: mischief causing damage to public property: imprisonment up to 5 years and fine; s.4: mischief causing damage to public property by fire or explosive substance: 1 to 10 years. The Supreme Court in Re: Destruction of Public and Private Properties (2009) and Kodungallur Film Society v UoI (2018) laid down directions, including setting up of liability on the organisers.

Tehseen S. Poonawalla v Union of India (2018): the Supreme Court condemned mob lynching and 'cow vigilantism' and issued preventive, remedial and punitive guidelines: appointment of a nodal officer in each district; FIR registration; fast-track trials; victim compensation; and directed Parliament to create a separate offence of lynching. BNS s.103(2) is Parliament's response; s.117(4) addresses mob grievous hurt. Subsequent follow up: Supreme Court in Nizam v Union of India (2024) reviewed compliance [VERIFY].

items.item: BNS, BNSS and BSA came into force on 1 July 2024; offences before that date remain governed by the IPC.

Delhi Race Club (1940) Ltd v State of UP: Supreme Court on the distinction between cheating and criminal breach of trust and against criminalising civil disputes.

items.exam_use: Rule of law, Art. 21 and criminal process.

Imran Pratapgadhi v State of Gujarat (Supreme Court): the Court quashed an FIR over a poem posted on social media and reiterated that speech must be judged by the standard of a reasonable, strong-minded person; free speech and the application of ss.196/197/299 BNS.

practice_scenarios.note: Application-style problems of the type AIBE uses. Each has a model answer with the rule and the reason.

items.scenario: A fires at B intending to kill him. The bullet misses B and kills C, a bystander.
items.answer: A is guilty of murder of C. Doctrine of transferred malice: BNS 102 (IPC 301) treats the offence as if the person intended to be killed had been killed. Punishment under BNS 103.

items.scenario: A and B quarrel suddenly in a market. B draws a knife; A snatches it and stabs B once in the chest, causing death. There was no premeditation.
items.answer: Exception 4 to BNS 101 (sudden fight) applies if A did not take undue advantage or act cruelly; A is liable for culpable homicide not amounting to murder (BNS 105). If A had inflicted several blows after B was disarmed, undue advantage would be shown and the exception fails.

items.scenario: A learns that his wife is having an affair. Three hours later, after a long reflection, he kills her.
items.answer: Murder. Grave and sudden provocation requires that the offender had no time to cool down; the passage of time and deliberation defeat the exception (Nanavati).

items.scenario: A shopkeeper is asked by Z to keep Rs 50,000 safely. He uses it to pay his own debts.
items.answer: Criminal breach of trust (BNS 316): entrustment plus dishonest use in violation of the trust.

items.scenario: A finds a gold chain on the road, takes it home and a week later, knowing the owner, sells it.
items.answer: Dishonest misappropriation of property (BNS 314): possession was innocent; dishonest intention arose later. If he knew the owner from the beginning and picked it up with dishonest intention, it is theft.

items.scenario: Four armed men break into a house and rob the owner at knifepoint.
items.answer: Robbery (BNS 309), not dacoity, because dacoity requires five or more persons.

items.scenario: A sends a message to Z: 'Pay Rs 5 lakh or I will release your private photographs.' Z pays.
items.answer: Extortion (BNS 308): putting a person in fear of injury (to reputation) and dishonestly inducing delivery of property; also criminal intimidation (BNS 351). If the threat is of sexual nature with images of a woman, voyeurism or IT Act provisions may also apply.

items.scenario: A doctor performs a procedure with a recognised technique, but the patient dies from a known, unavoidable complication.
items.answer: No criminal liability: Jacob Mathew requires gross negligence or recklessness. BNS 106(1) proviso caps punishment at 2 years for a registered medical practitioner even where negligence is proved; simple negligence gives rise to civil liability only.

items.scenario: A drunk driver hits a pedestrian and flees without informing the police or magistrate. The pedestrian dies.
items.answer: BNS 106(2) (hit and run): causing death by rash and negligent driving not amounting to culpable homicide and escaping without reporting: up to 10 years and fine. If the driver had knowledge that death was likely (e.g., extreme drunken driving at high speed in a crowded area), culpable homicide not amounting to murder (BNS 105 Part II) may be charged (Alister Anthony Pareira). Note the position on the implementation of s.106(2) [VERIFY].

items.scenario: A and B have been in a consensual relationship for two years. A promised marriage honestly but later marries someone else under family pressure. B alleges rape.
items.answer: No rape on these facts. Consent given on a promise made in good faith that later was broken is not obtained by a 'misconception of fact'; the promise must have been false from the inception (Uday; Pramod Pawar; Naim Ahamed). BNS 69 requires deceitful means including a promise made without any intention of fulfilling it.

items.scenario: Within 5 years of marriage a woman dies of burns at her matrimonial home. Her family says the husband and his parents demanded a car repeatedly until a week before the death.
items.answer: Dowry death (BNS 80(2)): death otherwise than in normal circumstances within seven years, with cruelty for dowry soon before death. The court presumes that the husband and relatives caused the dowry death (BSA s.118). Minimum 7 years, up to life. Cruelty (BNS 85) may also be charged; abetment of suicide (BNS 108) is an alternative with the presumption in BSA s.117.

items.scenario: Six persons stop a vehicle on suspicion that it carries beef, drag out the driver and beat him to death.
items.answer: Mob lynching: BNS 103(2) applies where five or more persons acting in concert commit murder on the ground of race, caste, community, sex, place of birth, language, personal belief or any similar ground. Death or life imprisonment and fine. Also unlawful assembly/rioting (BNS 189-191).

items.scenario: A mixes poison in B's tea intending to kill him. B notices the smell and does not drink it.
items.answer: Attempt to murder (BNS 109): the act of mixing poison with intent to kill is a step beyond preparation; if the tea had been handed to B, the last act would be done; either way the act is proximate. Up to 10 years and fine.

items.scenario: A child aged 6 takes a toy from a shop without paying.
items.answer: No offence: a child below 7 has absolute immunity (BNS 20).

items.scenario: A in a state of unsoundness of mind, believing he is cutting a log, kills B.
items.answer: Protected by BNS 22 (insanity) if, at the time of the act, he was incapable of knowing the nature of the act. The burden is on A to prove unsoundness at the time of the act by a preponderance of probabilities; legal, not medical, insanity is required.

items.scenario: A, at gunpoint, is ordered by robbers to drive their getaway car.
items.answer: Compulsion (BNS 32): a threat of instant death excuses the act except murder and offences against the State punishable with death; the threat must be present and continuing, and the person must not have voluntarily placed himself in the situation.

items.scenario: A buys goods from a company on the basis of a contract signed by the managing director, though the board's resolution authorising it was never passed.
items.answer: The company is bound if A acted in good faith and had no notice of the irregularity: the rule of indoor management (Royal British Bank v Turquand). It does not protect A if he had notice, or if the document was forged (Ruben v Great Fingall).

items.scenario: A public company held its last AGM on 30 September 2025. It wants to hold the next AGM on 15 January 2027.
items.answer: Not permissible: the gap between two AGMs cannot exceed 15 months (s.96), and the AGM for FY ending 31 March 2026 must be held within six months (by 30 September 2026). The Registrar may extend the time by up to three months for reasons shown, but not beyond that.

items.scenario: An operational creditor is owed Rs 80 lakh and wants to initiate CIRP.
items.answer: Not maintainable at present: the minimum amount of default is Rs 1 crore (notification dated 24 March 2020). The creditor may pursue ordinary recovery remedies.

items.scenario: A private company refuses to register a transfer of shares without giving reasons.
items.answer: A private company's articles can restrict transfer, but if the refusal is in contravention of the articles or the Act, the transferor or transferee may appeal to the NCLT within 30 days of the refusal or within 60 days from the date of delivery of the instrument if the company has not responded (s.58(3)-(4)).

items.scenario: Directors of a listed company approve a loan of Rs 10 crore to the managing director's brother's firm without disclosing the relationship.

open_book_use: AIBE permits bare Acts. Mark the first page of each Chapter and the index of BNS, BNSS, BSA and the Companies Act with tabs; add a page of your own mapping table inside the bare act if permitted by the latest BCI rules [VERIFY the current rule on annotated bare acts].
Do not use the bare act to search for a section you have never seen; use it to confirm the number, the minimum or maximum punishment and the wording of exceptions.
For MCQs naming a case, link the case to a one-line rule; for those naming a section, check the bare act in seconds, then move on.
Attempt all questions; there is no negative marking in the pattern as understood [VERIFY].
Time: about 3 hours for 100 questions: roughly 1.8 minutes per question; park the hard ones and return.
elimination_tactics: Extreme words (always, never, only) often signal a wrong option.
When two options differ only in number (5 years v 7 years), recall the structure of the offence (basic v aggravated).
For 'which is not', test each option against the definition; the exception usually comes from a neighbouring section.
For statements, mark each as true or false before reading the combinations.
